meanings: (of a bird, animal or plant) male

components.note: 牛 (ox, cattle) — 牡 refers to the male of an animal.
土 (tǔ) gives a sound distantly related to mǔ, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 牡丹花很漂亮。
example.pinyin: Mǔdan huā hěn piàoliang.
example.english: Peony flowers are very beautiful.
example.fact: 牡丹 (the peony) has been called China's 'king of flowers' for over a thousand years, with the city of Luoyang especially famous for its peony cultivation and annual peony festival.

etymologyHint: To bind 叕 by thread 纟; 叕 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 纟 depicts twisted thread; it signals that 缀 is about connecting or stitching things together.
叕 shows several linked pieces, reinforcing the idea of joining separate parts into one.

example.hanzi: 星星点缀着夜空。
example.pinyin: Xīngxīng diǎnzhuì zhe yèkōng.
example.english: Stars dot the night sky.
example.fact: 点缀 (diǎnzhuì) literally means 'dot-connect' and is a common Chinese word for small decorative touches, like scattered stars in the sky or a few flowers set into a garden.

etymologyHint: To pace 彳 back and forth 回; 回 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 彳 is the 'step' radical, marking 徊 as related to walking or movement.
回 means 'to return, to circle back'; its reading is close to huái, and its meaning reinforces the idea of pacing to and fro rather than heading somewhere directly.

example.hanzi: 他在门口徘徊了很久。
example.pinyin: Tā zài ménkǒu páihuái le hěn jiǔ.
example.english: He lingered at the doorway for a long time.
example.fact: 徊 almost never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists mainly in the pair 徘徊 (páihuái, 'to pace back and forth' or 'to waver'), rarely standing by itself.

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — 梨 is a fruit that grows on a tree.
利 (lì) gives a sound close to lí, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 我喜欢吃梨。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuān chī lí.
example.english: I like to eat pears.
example.fact: In Chinese culture it's considered unlucky to split a pear (分梨, fēnlí) with a partner or friend, because it sounds exactly like 分离 (fēnlí), 'to separate' — a classic homophone-based superstition.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 肪 is a kind of body fat.
方 (fāng) gives a sound close to fáng, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 鱼肉脂肪含量很低。
example.pinyin: Yúròu zhīfáng hánliàng hěn dī.
example.english: Fish meat has a low fat content.
example.fact: 肪 almost never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it exists mainly inside the compound 脂肪 (zhīfáng), the standard biology and nutrition term for 'fat.'

components.note: 氵 (water) — 涕 (in its literary sense) refers to tears.
弟 (dì) gives a sound distantly related to tì, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他感冒了,一直流鼻涕。
example.pinyin: Tā gǎnmào le, yīzhí liú bítì.
example.english: He caught a cold and keeps having a runny nose.
example.fact: 涕 originally meant 'tears' in classical Chinese (as in 痛哭流涕, 'weeping bitterly'), but in modern Mandarin it usually refers to nasal mucus, as in 鼻涕 (bítì, 'snot') — its core meaning shifted from the eyes to the nose over time.

components.note: 思 (to think, to ponder) — 惫 describes a mentally and physically worn-out state.
夂 (zhǐ) gives a sound only distantly related to bèi today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 加班之后他感到很疲惫。
example.pinyin: Jiābān zhīhòu tā gǎndào hěn píbèi.
example.english: After working overtime, he felt very exhausted.
example.fact: 惫 rarely stands alone in modern Chinese; it almost always appears in the compound 疲惫 (píbèi, 'exhausted'), pairing with 疲, which also means 'tired.'

components.note: 手 (hand) — 摹 means to trace or copy by hand.
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to mó, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他摹仿名家的字画。
example.pinyin: Tā mófǎng míngjiā de zìhuà.
example.english: He copies the calligraphy and paintings of famous masters.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese art training, 摹 (mó) meant tracing directly over a master's painting or calligraphy — a distinct technique from 临 (lín), copying freehand while looking at the original beside you.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 踱 describes a slow, foot-driven pace.
度 (dù) gives a sound distantly related to duó, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 他在花园里踱步沉思。
example.pinyin: Tā zài huāyuán lǐ duóbù chénsī.
example.english: He paced slowly through the garden, deep in thought.
example.fact: 踱 carries the foot radical 足, part of a family of Chinese characters describing specific manners of walking — like 跑 (run), 跳 (jump), and 蹲 (squat) — all built on the same root.

meanings: help a person shoulder a load
etymologyHint: A arm carrying an object 寸 at the side of the body ⺼

components.note: ⺼ is a variant of 肉/月 meaning 'flesh' or body part, marking 肘 as related to the body.
寸 ('inch') sits at the joint to mark a specific point on the arm — much as a measurement mark locates a spot on a ruler.

example.hanzi: 他的肘部撞到了桌子。
example.pinyin: Tā de zhǒubù zhuàng dào le zhuōzi.
example.english: His elbow bumped into the table.
example.fact: In cooking, 肘子 (zhǒuzi) refers to a braised pork knuckle or hock, a popular dish in Chinese cuisine such as 红烧肘子 — extending the body-part meaning of 肘 to a specific cut of meat.

etymologyHint: To form 容 hot metal 火; 容 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) marks that 熔 is about the effect of intense heat.
容 (róng) means 'to hold, to contain' and happens to share 熔's exact reading; the sense of holding evokes molten metal being contained in a vessel.

example.hanzi: 铁在高温下会熔化。
example.pinyin: Tiě zài gāowēn xià huì rónghuà.
example.english: Iron will melt at high temperatures.
example.fact: 熔 is used specifically for melting solids like metal or rock (熔岩, 'lava'; 熔点, 'melting point'), distinct from the near-homophone 溶 (róng, 'to dissolve in liquid') — a common mix-up for Chinese learners.

etymologyHint: To shake 执 hands 手; 执 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 手 (hand) grounds the character in a physical, hands-on gesture, like a firm handshake.
执 means 'to hold, to grasp'; paired with 手 it reinforces the image of holding on firmly, extended metaphorically to sincere, devoted feeling.

example.hanzi: 他们是一对挚友。
example.pinyin: Tāmen shì yī duì zhìyǒu.
example.english: They are a pair of close friends.
example.fact: 挚 appears in 挚友 (zhìyǒu, 'devoted friend') and 真挚 (zhēnzhì, 'sincere'), both describing deep emotional sincerity — its hand radical underscores the image of a firm, warm grasp.

components.note: 气 (gas, vapor) — 氯 (chlorine) is a gas.
录 (lù) gives a sound distantly related to lǜ, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 游泳池的水里有氯的味道。
example.pinyin: Yóuyǒngchí de shuǐ lǐ yǒu lǜ de wèidào.
example.english: The water in the swimming pool smells of chlorine.
example.fact: Swimming pools' characteristic smell doesn't actually come from pure chlorine (氯) — it comes from chloramines formed when chlorine reacts with organic contaminants in the water, like sweat and urine.

meanings: to shiver with cold or fear

components.note: 冫 (ice) — 凛 describes a bitter, icy cold or a chill of fear.
禀 (bǐng) gives a sound only distantly related to lǐn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 冬天的风凛冽刺骨。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān de fēng lǐnliè cìgǔ.
example.english: The winter wind is bitterly cold, cutting to the bone.
example.fact: 凛 carries the ice radical 冫, the same radical found in 冷 (cold), 冰 (ice), and 凉 (cool) — a small but reliable visual clue that a character relates to cold.

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 绎 (to unravel silk, to interpret) traces to drawing out a single continuous thread.

example.hanzi: 老师详细地演绎了这个理论。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī xiángxì de yǎnyì le zhège lǐlùn.
example.english: The teacher thoroughly elaborated on this theory.
example.fact: 演绎 (yǎnyì) is the standard Chinese term for logical 'deduction,' paired against 归纳 (guīnà, 'induction') — mirroring the same deductive-versus-inductive distinction used in Western logic.

etymologyHint: Many people 灬 (twenty or more 廿) in a house 广

components.note: 广 depicts a simple shelter or building — many characters using this radical relate to structures.
廿 means 'twenty'; grouped with the dots beneath it under the roof, it suggests a large gathering of people, giving 庶 its sense of 'numerous, multitude.'

example.hanzi: 庶民百姓都盼望着好日子。
example.pinyin: Shùmín bǎixìng dōu pànwàng zhe hǎo rìzi.
example.english: Ordinary common people all hope for a good life.
example.fact: In imperial China, 庶民 (shùmín) referred to the common people as opposed to nobility and officials — 庶 by itself meant 'numerous' partly because commoners vastly outnumbered the ruling class.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 脯 (as in 胸脯) names a fleshy part of the body.
甫 (fǔ) gives a sound distantly related to pú, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他挺起胸脯,充满自信。
example.pinyin: Tā tǐng qǐ xiōngpú, chōngmǎn zìxìn.
example.english: He puffed out his chest, full of confidence.
example.fact: 脯 has two different pronunciations depending on meaning: pú in 胸脯 (xiōngpú, 'chest'), but fǔ in 果脯 (guǒfǔ, 'candied/preserved fruit') — the same character shifting sound along with sense.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 迭 describes something happening repeatedly, one after another.
失 (shī) gives a sound only distantly related to dié today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 公司的产品每年都在迭代更新。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī de chǎnpǐn měinián dōu zài diédài gēngxīn.
example.english: The company's product is updated iteratively every year.
example.fact: 迭代 (diédài, 'iteration') is the standard Chinese term used in computer science and engineering for repeating a process step by step — the same concept used in software development worldwide.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 睦 (harmony) is traditionally framed as living peaceably in one's neighbors' sight.
坴 (lù) gives a sound distantly related to mù, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 邻居之间应该和睦相处。
example.pinyin: Línjū zhījiān yīnggāi hémù xiāngchǔ.
example.english: Neighbors should get along harmoniously.
example.fact: 和睦 (hémù, 'harmonious') is a key term in traditional Chinese family and social values, rooted in the Confucian emphasis on social harmony between neighbors, siblings, and even nations.

meanings: (fig.) key (to the solution of a problem)

components.note: 穴 (cave, hole) — 窍 (a knack, an opening) is literally a small hole.
巧 (qiǎo) gives a sound close to qiào, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他终于找到了解决问题的窍门。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú zhǎodào le jiějué wèntí de qiàomén.
example.english: He finally found the trick to solving the problem.
example.fact: 窍门 (qiàomén) literally means an 'opening, a gate,' but idiomatically means 'the knack' or 'the trick' — as if a hard problem were a locked space needing the right opening to get through easily.

meanings: used in 葷粥|荤粥[Xun1 yu4]

components.note: 米 (rice) is the central ingredient being cooked.
The curved strokes flanking the rice are thought to depict the pot, or the steam rising as the rice simmers into a thick gruel.

example.hanzi: 我早饭喜欢喝小米粥。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zǎofàn xǐhuān hē xiǎomǐ zhōu.
example.english: I like to drink millet congee for breakfast.
example.fact: Congee (粥, zhōu) is a staple breakfast food across China and much of East Asia, often eaten plain or paired with pickled vegetables, salted egg, or preserved tofu for being easy to digest.

etymologyHint: A building 广 where people remain 奄; 奄 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 广 shows a simple roof or shelter, marking 庵 as a type of building.
奄 means 'to cover, to remain'; here it suggests a modest dwelling where someone stays in quiet retreat — fitting for a small hermitage.

example.hanzi: 山上有一座小庵。
example.pinyin: Shān shàng yǒu yī zuò xiǎo ān.
example.english: There is a small nunnery on the mountain.
example.fact: 庵 traditionally refers to a small Buddhist convent or hermitage, often for nuns, distinct from 寺 (sì), which usually denotes a larger temple, frequently for monks.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沧 describes the vast blue-green of open water.
仓 (cāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 沧's reading.

example.hanzi: 他经历了人生的沧桑。
example.pinyin: Tā jīnglì le rénshēng de cāngsāng.
example.english: He has experienced life's ups and downs.
example.fact: 沧桑 (cāngsāng), short for 沧海桑田 ('a blue sea turning into mulberry fields'), is an ancient idiom about dramatic change over vast stretches of time, now used for the hardships and transformations of a lifetime.

components.note: 心 (heart, mind) — 怠 (laziness, negligence) is a state of mind.
台 (tái) gives a sound distantly related to dài, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 服务员对顾客怠慢无礼。
example.pinyin: Fúwùyuán duì gùkè dàimàn wúlǐ.
example.english: The waiter was neglectful and rude to the customer.
example.fact: 怠 shares its sense of 'laziness, negligence' with 懈怠 (xièdài, 'to slack off'); both are built on the heart radical 心, reflecting how Chinese characters often locate mental and emotional states in the heart.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沁 describes a liquid or scent gently seeping in.
心 (xīn) gives a sound distantly related to qìn, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 花香沁人心脾。
example.pinyin: Huāxiāng qìn rén xīn pí.
example.english: The fragrance of the flowers is deeply refreshing.
example.fact: The idiom 沁人心脾 (qìn rén xīn pí) literally describes a sensation 'seeping into the heart and spleen,' and is used for a scent, taste, or piece of music so pleasant it feels like it permeates one's whole being.

components.note: 大 (big) — 奕 conveys a sense of grandness.
亦 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 奕's reading.

example.hanzi: 老人虽然年迈,却神采奕奕。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén suīrán niánmài, què shén cǎi yì yì.
example.english: Although the old man is elderly, he looks radiant and full of spirit.
example.fact: 神采奕奕 (shéncǎi yìyì) is a common compliment in Chinese describing someone who looks vibrant and full of life — 奕 by itself rarely appears outside this and similar reduplicated expressions.

meanings: used in 喉嚨|喉咙[hou2 long2]

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咙 (as in 喉咙) names the throat, an opening in the body.
龙 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 咙's reading.

example.hanzi: 他喉咙痛,说不出话来。
example.pinyin: Tā hóulóng tòng, shuō bu chū huà lái.
example.english: His throat hurts, and he can't speak.
example.fact: 咙 almost never appears alone; it exists specifically as the second syllable of 喉咙 (hóulóng, 'throat') — a common Chinese wordbuilding pattern where two near-synonymous characters combine into one word.

components.note: 气 (gas, vapor) — 氨 (ammonia) is a gas.
安 (ān) gives the sound — an exact match with 氨's reading.

example.hanzi: 氨是一种有强烈气味的气体。
example.pinyin: Ān shì yī zhǒng yǒu qiángliè qìwèi de qìtǐ.
example.english: Ammonia is a gas with a strong smell.
example.fact: Ammonia (氨, ān) is a key industrial chemical used to make nitrogen fertilizer, and the Haber-Bosch process for synthesizing it from nitrogen and hydrogen gas is credited with dramatically increasing global food production in the 20th century.

etymologyHint: Three people standing up straight 直

components.note: 矗 stacks three copies of 直 ('straight') to intensify the meaning into 'towering, upright' — the same repetition trick used in 森 (three 木 'tree' = forest).

example.hanzi: 高楼矗立在城市中心。
example.pinyin: Gāolóu chùlì zài chéngshì zhōngxīn.
example.english: Tall buildings stand erect in the city center.
example.fact: 矗 is made of three copies of 直 ('straight') stacked together — tripling a character is a common way Chinese intensifies meaning, similar to how 森 (forest) stacks three 木 (tree).

components.note: 皿 (dish, vessel) — 盔 (a helmet) is a rounded, bowl-like vessel worn on the head.
灰 (huī) gives a sound distantly related to kuī, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 骑摩托车要戴头盔。
example.pinyin: Qí mótuōchē yào dài tóukuī.
example.english: You must wear a helmet when riding a motorcycle.
example.fact: 盔 shares its bowl-shaped radical 皿 with characters like 盆 (basin) and 盘 (plate) — a family of characters that all denote open, rounded vessels, matching a helmet's curved shape.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拇 (the thumb) is a part of the hand.
母 (mǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 拇's reading.

example.hanzi: 他竖起大拇指表示赞赏。
example.pinyin: Tā shùqǐ dà mǔzhǐ biǎoshì zànshǎng.
example.english: He gave a thumbs-up to show approval.
example.fact: 拇指 (mǔzhǐ) is the only finger with its own dedicated root character — the other fingers are typically just numbered or described (食指 index, 中指 middle, 无名指 ring, 小指 pinky) rather than named with a unique character like 拇.

etymologyHint: Circulating 巿 water 氵, representing a flood

components.note: 氵 (water) sets the character in the domain of liquids and flow.
巿 suggests something spreading or circulating widely; combined with water, it builds the sense of water flowing abundantly — hence 'copious, abundant.'

example.hanzi: 年轻人应该精力充沛。
example.pinyin: Niánqīng rén yīnggāi jīnglì chōngpèi.
example.english: Young people should be full of energy.
example.fact: 沛 is part of the ancient place name 沛县 in Jiangsu province, the hometown of Liu Bang, founder of the Han dynasty — one of many Chinese characters that double as both descriptive words and place names.

etymologyHint: A bed of wood 木 and feathers 羽 to sleep in at night 日

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 榻 as a wooden piece of furniture.
羽 (feather) suggests softness, as in bedding to sleep on.

example.hanzi: 他病重,一直躺在病榻上。
example.pinyin: Tā bìngzhòng, yīzhí tǎng zài bìngtà shàng.
example.english: He is gravely ill and has been lying in his sickbed.
example.fact: The classical term 下榻 (xiàtà, literally 'to get off the couch') is still used today as a formal, polite way to say someone is lodging somewhere, especially for VIP guests in news reports about visiting officials.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揣 describes tucking something with the hand.
耑 (duān) gives a sound only distantly related to chuāi today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他把手揣在袖子里取暖。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shǒu chuāi zài xiùzi lǐ qǔnuǎn.
example.english: He tucked his hands into his sleeves for warmth.
example.fact: 揣 has two distinct pronunciations for two distinct meanings: chuāi means to tuck something into your clothing, while chuǎi (as in 揣测, 'to speculate') means to guess or estimate.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崭 (towering, striking) is rooted in the image of a tall peak.
斩 (zhǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 崭's reading.

example.hanzi: 他买了一辆崭新的自行车。
example.pinyin: Tā mǎi le yī liàng zhǎnxīn de zìxíngchē.
example.english: He bought a brand-new bicycle.
example.fact: 崭新 (zhǎnxīn) is one of the most common ways to say 'brand-new' in Mandarin, pairing 崭 (originally 'towering, standing out') with 新 (new) to emphasize something strikingly fresh.

components.note: 革 (leather) — 鞘 (a sheath) is traditionally leather-wrapped.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound distantly related to qiào, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他把剑放回鞘中。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ jiàn fàng huí qiào zhōng.
example.english: He put the sword back into its sheath.
example.fact: 鞘 uses the leather radical 革, found in many words for hide-based gear like 鞋 (shoe) and 鞍 (saddle) — reflecting that traditional scabbards were often leather-wrapped wood.

components.note: 革 (leather) — 鞠 (to bow) traces to leather-ball games and bending the body; 革 anchors the character materially.
匊 (jū) gives the sound — an exact match with 鞠's reading.

example.hanzi: 学生们向老师鞠躬行礼。
example.pinyin: Xuéshēngmen xiàng lǎoshī jūgōng xínglǐ.
example.english: The students bowed to the teacher as a greeting.
example.fact: 鞠躬 (jūgōng), the standard word for 'to bow,' is part of required formal etiquette in many Chinese contexts, from graduation ceremonies to business meetings, where the depth and duration of the bow can signal respect.

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 垦 (to cultivate land) is an act performed on soil.
艮 (gěn) gives a sound distantly related to kěn, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 农民开垦了一片荒地。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín kāikěn le yī piàn huāngdì.
example.english: The farmers reclaimed a stretch of wasteland for farming.
example.fact: 北大荒 ('Great Northern Wasteland') in Heilongjiang was a major site of state-organized land reclamation (开垦) in the mid-20th century, transforming vast marshland into one of China's most productive grain-producing regions.

etymologyHint: To combine 合 two solutions 氵

components.note: 氵 (water) suggests smooth mixing, as liquids blend easily together.
合 means 'to combine, to fit together'; paired with water, it evokes two things merging smoothly — hence 'harmonious, in accord.'

example.hanzi: 双方就合作事宜进行了洽谈。
example.pinyin: Shuāngfāng jiù hézuò shìyí jìnxíng le qiàtán.
example.english: Both sides held talks about the cooperation matter.
example.fact: 洽谈 (qiàtán) is standard business Chinese for 'to hold discussions or negotiations,' frequently seen in trade and diplomacy contexts, such as 洽谈会 (a business negotiation fair).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唾 (saliva, to spit) comes from the mouth.
垂 (chuí) gives a sound only distantly related to tuò today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他对这种行为感到唾弃。
example.pinyin: Tā duì zhè zhǒng xíngwéi gǎndào tuòqì.
example.english: He feels utter contempt for this kind of behavior.
example.fact: 唾弃 (tuòqì), literally 'to spit and abandon,' is a strong idiom for showing scorn — spitting has long carried a symbolic meaning of disdain across many cultures, including China's.

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 cabinet 厨; 厨 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 橱 as a wooden piece of furniture.
厨 means 'kitchen'; the character's original sense was a kitchen cupboard, later broadening to cabinets of any kind.

example.hanzi: 她把衣服放进衣橱里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yīfu fàng jìn yīchú lǐ.
example.english: She put the clothes into the wardrobe.
example.fact: 橱 combines the wood radical 木 with 厨 (kitchen) — the character's original sense was a kitchen cupboard (橱柜) before extending to cabinets and wardrobes of any kind.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 仕 (to serve as an official) describes a role held by a person.
士 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 仕's reading.

example.hanzi: 他年轻时就步入仕途。
example.pinyin: Tā niánqīng shí jiù bùrù shìtú.
example.english: He entered an official career while still young.
example.fact: In imperial China, passing the 科举 civil-service examinations was the primary path to 仕途 (shìtú, 'an official career') — a system that lasted over 1,300 years, from the Sui dynasty until it was abolished in 1905.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蜘 (as in 蜘蛛, spider) names a small crawling creature.
知 (zhī) gives the sound — an exact match with 蜘's reading.

example.hanzi: 墙角有一只蜘蛛。
example.pinyin: Qiángjiǎo yǒu yī zhī zhīzhū.
example.english: There is a spider in the corner of the wall.
example.fact: 蜘 never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists solely as the first syllable of 蜘蛛 (zhīzhū, 'spider'), a two-character word where neither character has an independent meaning on its own.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痰 (phlegm) is a symptom tied to illness.
炎 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to tán, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 医生让他把痰咳出来检查。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng ràng tā bǎ tán ké chūlái jiǎnchá.
example.english: The doctor had him cough up phlegm for examination.
example.fact: 痰 carries the sickness radical 疒, seen in dozens of characters for ailments and symptoms, such as 病 (illness), 痛 (pain), and 疲 (fatigue) — a reliable visual cue that a word relates to health.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 袜 (socks) are an item of clothing.
末 (mò) gives a sound only distantly related to wà today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 冬天要穿厚一点的袜子。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān yào chuān hòu yī diǎn de wàzi.
example.english: In winter you should wear slightly thicker socks.
example.fact: 袜 carries the clothing radical 衤(a compact form of 衣), shared with characters like 裤 (pants) and 衫 (shirt) — visually distinguished from the similar-looking spirit radical 礻 by just one small stroke.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峙 (to stand erect) is rooted in the image of a mountain standing firm.
寺 (sì) gives a sound distantly related to zhì, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 两国军队在边境对峙。
example.pinyin: Liǎng guó jūnduì zài biānjìng duìzhì.
example.english: The two countries' armies are in a standoff at the border.
example.fact: 对峙 (duìzhì) is common in news Chinese for tense standoffs — military, political, or even a personal argument — extending the literal image of two mountains standing opposite each other.

meanings: abbr. for 柬埔寨[Jian3 pu3 zhai4], Cambodia

components.note: 束 means 'to bind, a bundle' — like a bundle of bamboo slips tied together, the traditional material for written notes and letters.

example.hanzi: 他收到了一张结婚请柬。
example.pinyin: Tā shōudào le yī zhāng jiéhūn qǐngjiǎn.
example.english: He received a wedding invitation.
example.fact: 柬 is also the character used to transliterate 'Cambodia' (柬埔寨, Jiǎnpǔzhài) in Chinese, unrelated in meaning to its original sense of a written note — a common way Chinese repurposes characters purely for sound in foreign place names.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蝉 (the cicada) is an insect.
单 (dān) gives a sound distantly related to chán, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 夏天树上有很多蝉在叫。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān shù shàng yǒu hěn duō chán zài jiào.
example.english: In summer, there are many cicadas calling in the trees.
example.fact: The loud, continuous chirping of cicadas (蝉鸣, chánmíng) is such a strong seasonal marker in China that it became a common poetic symbol for summer in classical Chinese poetry over a thousand years ago.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蟹 (the crab) is a small shelled creature classed with insects in traditional radical schemes.
解 (jiě) gives a sound distantly related to xiè, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 秋天是吃大闸蟹的好季节。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān shì chī dàzháxiè de hǎo jìjié.
example.english: Autumn is a good season for eating hairy crabs.
example.fact: 大闸蟹 ('hairy crab'), especially from Yangcheng Lake near Suzhou, is one of China's most prized autumn delicacies, and its short yearly harvest season drives intense seasonal demand.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谏 (to remonstrate) is done through speech.
柬 (jiǎn) gives a sound close to jiàn, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 大臣向皇帝进谏。
example.pinyin: Dàchén xiàng huángdì jìnjiàn.
example.english: The minister offered candid advice to the emperor.
example.fact: In imperial China, 进谏 — a court official respectfully criticizing or advising the emperor — was an institutionalized practice, and some dynasties even had dedicated 'remonstrance officials' (谏官) whose formal job was to challenge the ruler's decisions.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹃 (the cuckoo) is a bird.
肙 (yuàn) gives a sound distantly related to juān, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 山上开满了杜鹃花。
example.pinyin: Shān shàng kāi mǎn le dùjuānhuā.
example.english: The mountain is covered in blooming azaleas.
example.fact: 杜鹃 (dùjuān) is a rare case where one word names two unrelated things — the cuckoo bird and the azalea flower — linked only by a legend of a heartbroken king who turned into a cuckoo whose cries stained flowers red.

meanings: to raise; to hold up; to lift up

components.note: 手 (hand) — 擎 (to lift, to hold up) is an act done with the hand.
敬 (jìng) gives a sound distantly related to qíng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 这台引擎的动力很强。
example.pinyin: Zhè tái yǐnqíng de dònglì hěn qiáng.
example.english: This engine's power is very strong.
example.fact: 引擎 (yǐnqíng, 'engine') is a phonetic loanword — 擎 was chosen mainly because it sounds like '-gine,' not for its original meaning of 'to hold up, to lift,' showing how Chinese sometimes borrows characters purely for sound.

components.note: 白 (white) — 皓 (bright, luminous) describes a pure, clear whiteness.
告 (gào) gives a sound distantly related to hào, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 皓月当空,格外明亮。
example.pinyin: Hàoyuè dāng kōng, géwài míngliàng.
example.english: The bright moon hangs in the sky, especially luminous.
example.fact: 皓 is a popular character in Chinese given names, especially for boys, because of its bright, luminous, and auspicious connotations — often paired with characters meaning 'sky' or 'moon.'

example.hanzi: 朕决定亲征。
example.pinyin: Zhèn juédìng qīnzhēng.
example.english: We (the emperor) have decided to lead the campaign in person.
example.fact: Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, decreed in 221 BC that 朕 (zhèn) would be reserved exclusively for the emperor's own use as 'I/We' — a linguistic monopoly on a single pronoun that lasted until the fall of the last dynasty in 1912.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 疤 (a scar) is a mark left by injury, grouped with sickness-related characters.
巴 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 疤's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的手臂上有一道疤。
example.pinyin: Tā de shǒubì shàng yǒu yī dào bā.
example.english: There is a scar on his arm.
example.fact: 疤 uses the sickness radical 疒 even though a scar itself isn't an illness — the radical here marks any lasting mark left on the body by injury or disease.

example.hanzi: 他在番禺工作。
example.pinyin: Tā zài Pānyú gōngzuò.
example.english: He works in Panyu.
example.fact: 禺 originally referred to a type of monkey in ancient texts like the Shuowen Jiezi dictionary, though today it survives mainly in place names, such as 番禺 (Pānyú), a district of Guangzhou.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铲 (a shovel) is a metal tool.
产 (chǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 铲's reading.

example.hanzi: 他用铁铲挖土。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng tiěchǎn wā tǔ.
example.english: He used an iron shovel to dig earth.
example.fact: 铲 carries the metal radical 钅, used in nearly all Chinese words for metal tools and materials — from 锅 (wok) to 银 (silver) — a quick visual signal that something is metallic.

components.note: 酉 (wine) — 酶 (an enzyme) was classed by early chemists under the wine/fermentation radical.
每 (měi) gives a sound close to méi, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 消化需要各种酶的帮助。
example.pinyin: Xiāohuà xūyào gè zhǒng méi de bāngzhù.
example.english: Digestion requires the help of various enzymes.
example.fact: Enzymes (酶, méi) are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living cells without being consumed themselves — the human body relies on thousands of different enzymes just for digestion and metabolism.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钝 (blunt) describes a metal blade that has lost its edge.
屯 (tún) gives a sound distantly related to dùn, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 这把刀太钝了,切不动肉。
example.pinyin: Zhè bǎ dāo tài dùn le, qiè bu dòng ròu.
example.english: This knife is too blunt to cut through the meat.
example.fact: In geometry, 钝角 (dùnjiǎo, 'obtuse angle') describes any angle greater than 90° but less than 180°, borrowing 钝's everyday meaning of 'blunt' to describe a wide, non-sharp angle — the same metaphor English uses with 'obtuse.'

components.note: 民 (people) — 氓 (the common people) refers to a nation's subjects.
亡 (wáng) gives a sound distantly related to máng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 古书中,氓指普通百姓。
example.pinyin: Gǔshū zhōng, máng zhǐ pǔtōng bǎixìng.
example.english: In ancient texts, 'máng' refers to ordinary common people.
example.fact: 氓 has two readings with very different meanings: in classical Chinese, máng meant 'the common people' (as in the ancient poem 氓 from the Book of Songs), while in modern Mandarin the same character is read méng in 流氓 (liúmáng, 'hooligan') — a striking shift from neutral to negative over two millennia.

components.note: 匚 (box) — 匣 (a small box) is itself a container.
甲 (jiǎ) gives a sound distantly related to xiá, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 她把首饰放进一个木匣里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shǒushì fàng jìn yī gè mù xiá lǐ.
example.english: She put her jewelry into a wooden box.
example.fact: 匣 carries the box-enclosure radical 匚, which visually wraps around the rest of the character like an open container — the same radical appears in 匠 (craftsman, originally a toolbox) and 匡 (to correct, to frame).

components.note: 弓 (bow) — 弧 (an arc) traces to the curve of a drawn bow.
瓜 (guā) gives a sound only distantly related to hú today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 篮球划出一道弧线飞进篮筐。
example.pinyin: Lánqiú huà chū yī dào húxiàn fēi jìn lánkuāng.
example.english: The basketball traced an arc through the air into the hoop.
example.fact: In mathematics, 弧度 (hùdù, 'radian') is the standard unit for measuring angles in higher math and physics, based on arc length — the character 弧 (arc) directly reflects the geometric idea of a curved segment of a circle.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峨 (lofty, towering) describes a mountain.
我 (wǒ) gives a sound only distantly related to é today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 峨眉山是中国四大佛教名山之一。
example.pinyin: Éméi Shān shì Zhōngguó sìdà fójiào míngshān zhī yī.
example.english: Mount Emei is one of China's four great Buddhist sacred mountains.
example.fact: Mount Emei (峨眉山) in Sichuan is one of the Four Sacred Buddhist Mountains of China and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, known for its Golden Summit and resident macaque monkeys.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锥 (a drill, an awl) is a metal tool.
隹 (zhuī) gives the sound — an exact match with 锥's reading.

example.hanzi: 冰淇淋放在圆锥形的蛋卷筒里。
example.pinyin: Bīngqílín fàng zài yuánzhuī xíng de dànjuǎn tǒng lǐ.
example.english: The ice cream is placed in a cone-shaped wafer cup.
example.fact: 圆锥 (yuánzhuī, 'cone') is the standard geometry term for a cone shape, combining 圆 ('round') with 锥, whose base meaning of 'awl, drill bit' already carries the image of a pointed, tapering shape.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揪 (to grasp, to pinch) is an act done with the hand.
秋 (qiū) gives a sound distantly related to jiū, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 这个消息让人很揪心。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi ràng rén hěn jiūxīn.
example.english: This news makes people feel anguished.
example.fact: 揪心 (jiūxīn), literally 'to grab or pinch the heart,' is a vivid Chinese expression for intense worry or anguish — using the physical image of something clutching at your heart, much like the English idiom 'heart-wrenching.'

etymologyHint: A wooden 木 lever 工; 工 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 木 (wood) marks 杠 as originally referring to a wooden pole or beam.
工 depicts a simple tool or work-implement shape; combined with wood, it reinforces the sense of a sturdy pole or bar used for lifting or carrying.

example.hanzi: 运动员在单杠上做体操动作。
example.pinyin: Yùndòngyuán zài dāngàng shàng zuò tǐcāo dòngzuò.
example.english: The athlete performs gymnastics moves on the horizontal bar.
example.fact: 单杠 (horizontal bar) and 双杠 (parallel bars) are two of the six apparatus events in men's Olympic artistic gymnastics.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 吭 (the throat) is an opening in the body used for speech.
亢 (kàng) gives a sound distantly related to kēng, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 他一声不吭地走了。
example.pinyin: Tā yī shēng bù kēng de zǒu le.
example.english: He left without saying a word.
example.fact: The idiom 一声不吭 ('not utter a single sound') is a common way in Mandarin to describe someone staying completely silent, often out of anger, resignation, or stubbornness.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崛 (to rise up abruptly) is rooted in the image of a mountain thrusting upward.
屈 (qū) gives a sound only distantly related to jué today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 中国经济近几十年迅速崛起。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó jīngjì jìn jǐ shí nián xùnsù juéqǐ.
example.english: China's economy has risen rapidly in recent decades.
example.fact: 崛起 (juéqǐ, 'to rise up, to emerge') is frequently used in Chinese media and academia to describe the rapid rise of a nation's economy, especially China's own growth since its reform and opening-up policies began in 1978.

etymologyHint: To start 讠 a witch-hunt 巫; 巫 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) marks 诬 as an act carried out through words.
巫 means 'witch, shaman'; paired with speech, it evokes casting a false, damaging accusation — like a curse spoken against someone.

example.hanzi: 他被诬陷偷了钱。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi wūxiàn tōu le qián.
example.english: He was falsely accused of stealing money.
example.fact: 诬告 (wūgào, 'false accusation') is itself a criminal offense under Chinese law — deliberately fabricating charges against someone can lead to prosecution, mirroring similar laws against false accusation found in many legal systems.

example.hanzi: 炊烟冉冉升起。
example.pinyin: Chuīyān rǎnrǎn shēngqǐ.
example.english: Cooking smoke gradually rises.
example.fact: 冉冉 (rǎnrǎn) is a poetic reduplicated form describing something rising or moving slowly and gently, such as smoke drifting upward or a flag rising — 冉 rarely appears as a single, standalone character outside this doubled form or as a surname.

components.note: 予 (to give) — 抒 (to express, to pour out) traces to bailing water out by hand.
扌 is tagged as the sound-carrying element here, though the hand radical usually serves a meaning role elsewhere in Chinese characters; its reading (shǒu) bears only a distant resemblance to shū.

example.hanzi: 这首诗抒发了作者的思乡之情。
example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu shī shūfā le zuòzhě de sīxiāng zhī qíng.
example.english: This poem expresses the poet's homesickness.
example.fact: 抒情 (shūqíng, 'lyrical, to express emotion') is a core term in Chinese literary criticism, classifying poetry and prose centered on personal feeling, as opposed to 叙事 (xùshì, 'narrative') writing that focuses on telling a story.

example.hanzi: 他和我同庚。
example.pinyin: Tā hé wǒ tónggēng.
example.english: He and I are the same age.
example.fact: 庚 is one of the ten Heavenly Stems (天干) that combine with the twelve Earthly Branches to form the 60-year sexagenary cycle traditionally used in China for counting years, such as in 庚子年 ('year of Geng-Zi,' e.g. 1900 and 1960).

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 悍 (fierce, bold) is a trait of temperament, seated in the heart.
旱 (hàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 悍's reading.

example.hanzi: 他性格强悍,从不服输。
example.pinyin: Tā xìnggé qiánghàn, cóng bù fúshū.
example.english: His personality is tough and fierce; he never admits defeat.
example.fact: 悍 combines the heart radical 忄 with fierce boldness, appearing in words describing both admirable courage (强悍, 'tough') and dangerous aggression (凶悍, 'fierce and violent') — the same root character can carry a positive or negative shade depending on context.

components.note: 非 (not, negative, non-; to oppose) — 靡 (here, extravagant) is framed as a negation of restraint.
麻 (má) gives a sound distantly related to mí, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 生活奢靡容易带来麻烦。
example.pinyin: Shēnghuó shēmí róngyì dàilái máfan.
example.english: An extravagant lifestyle can easily bring trouble.
example.fact: 靡 has two distinct pronunciations tied to different meanings: mí, as in 奢靡 (shēmí, 'extravagant, dissolute'), and mǐ, as in 风靡 (fēngmǐ, 'to sweep through, become a craze') — a single character bridging wasteful excess and unstoppable popularity.

meanings: (bound form) last day of a lunar month

components.note: 日 (sun) — 晦 (dark, obscure) describes a day with no sunlight.
每 (měi) gives a sound only distantly related to huì today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 这篇文章写得很晦涩,难以理解。
example.pinyin: Zhè piān wénzhāng xiě de hěn huìsè, nányǐ lǐjiě.
example.english: This article is written very obscurely and is hard to understand.
example.fact: 晦涩 (huìsè) is the standard term Chinese literary critics use for writing that is needlessly difficult, pairing 晦 ('dark, unclear') with 涩 ('rough, astringent') to describe prose that is hard to digest.

etymologyHint: Aged 昔 wine 酉; wine gone sour

components.note: 酉 is the wine radical, appearing in characters for fermented drinks and condiments.
昔 means 'formerly, long ago'; paired with the wine radical, it evokes wine that has aged for a long time — turning sour into vinegar.

example.hanzi: 她看到男朋友和别的女生说话就吃醋。
example.pinyin: Tā kàndào nánpéngyou hé bié de nǚshēng shuōhuà jiù chīcù.
example.english: She gets jealous when she sees her boyfriend talking to other girls.
example.fact: Chinese rice vinegar (醋, cù) has been produced for at least 2,000 years and is foundational to Chinese cuisine, forming the base for famous regional styles like Shanxi's aged vinegar (山西老陈醋).

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 壕 (a trench) is a channel dug into the earth.
豪 (háo) gives the sound — an exact match with 壕's reading.

example.hanzi: 士兵们躲在战壕里。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen duǒ zài zhànháo lǐ.
example.english: The soldiers hid in the trench.
example.fact: 战壕 ('battle trench') became a defining image of World War I, when opposing armies dug extensive trench networks along the Western Front, leading to years of grueling stalemate warfare.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锯 (a saw) is a metal-bladed tool.
居 (jū) gives a sound close to jù, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他用锯子把木头锯断。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng jùzi bǎ mùtou jù duàn.
example.english: He used a saw to cut the wood in two.
example.fact: 锯 uses the metal radical 钅, even though most handsaws have wooden handles — the radical points specifically to the metal blade, the part of the tool that actually does the cutting.

etymologyHint: A person with head tilted - leaning forward, running, energetic

example.hanzi: 这项计划因资金不足而夭折。
example.pinyin: Zhè xiàng jìhuà yīn zījīn bùzú ér yāozhé.
example.english: This plan fell through prematurely due to insufficient funding.
example.fact: 夭折 (yāozhé) literally means 'to die young,' but in modern Chinese it's frequently used metaphorically for a plan, project, or relationship that fails or is cut short before completion.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 咦 is a pure interjection made with the mouth.
夷 (yí) gives the sound — an exact match with 咦's reading.

example.hanzi: 咦,这是怎么回事?
example.pinyin: Yí, zhè shì zěnme huí shì?
example.english: Huh, what's going on here?
example.fact: 咦 is a pure interjection built on the mouth radical 口, part of a family of exclamation characters like 啊, 哦, and 呀 — all grounded in this radical since they represent sounds people make while reacting or speaking.

etymologyHint: A person 亻 with more than they need 多

components.note: 亻 (person radical) marks 侈 as describing a way a person behaves.
多 means 'many, more than enough'; combined with the person radical, it paints someone who indulges in more than they need — extravagant, wasteful.

example.hanzi: 他过着奢侈的生活。
example.pinyin: Tā guò zhe shēchǐ de shēnghuó.
example.english: He lives an extravagant lifestyle.
example.fact: 奢侈品 (shēchǐpǐn, 'luxury goods') is the standard Chinese term used in retail and economics for high-end luxury products — China has in recent decades become one of the world's largest markets for global luxury brands.

etymologyHint: A humble 卑 woman 女; 卑 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 (woman) marks 婢 as referring specifically to a female servant.
卑 means 'lowly, humble'; combined with 女, it reflects the low social status historically assigned to female servants.

example.hanzi: 古代大户人家常有奴婢伺候。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài dàhù rénjiā cháng yǒu núbì cìhòu.
example.english: Wealthy households in ancient times often had servants to attend to them.
example.fact: 奴婢 (núbì) was the historical term in imperial China for household servants, a legally recognized social class that only began to be abolished under reforms in the late Qing and early Republican periods.

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 猾 (crafty, cunning) was traditionally likened to a wild animal's slyness.
骨 (gǔ) gives a sound only distantly related to huá today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 这只狐狸非常狡猾。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī húli fēicháng jiǎohuá.
example.english: This fox is extremely cunning.
example.fact: 狡猾 (jiǎohuá, 'crafty, cunning') uses two characters that both carry the dog/beast radical 犭, since cunning behavior was traditionally likened in Chinese to that of foxes and other wild animals.

components.note: 彳 (to step with the left foot) — 徘 (as in 徘徊, to pace) describes an act of walking.
非 (fēi) gives a sound only distantly related to pái today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他在河边徘徊,不知该怎么办。
example.pinyin: Tā zài hébiān páihuái, bù zhī gāi zěnme bàn.
example.english: He paced back and forth by the river, not knowing what to do.
example.fact: 徘 and 徊 almost never appear apart — together they form 徘徊 (páihuái), describing aimless pacing or emotional wavering, and both halves share the 'step' radical 彳.

components.note: 石 (stone, rock, mineral) — 硝 (saltpeter) is a mineral.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound close to xiāo, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 硝酸是一种强腐蚀性的化学品。
example.pinyin: Xiāosuān shì yī zhǒng qiáng fǔshí xìng de huàxuépǐn.
example.english: Nitric acid is a highly corrosive chemical.
example.fact: Saltpeter (硝石, potassium nitrate) is one of the three key ingredients in gunpowder, alongside sulfur and charcoal — gunpowder was invented in China around the 9th century, reportedly by Taoist alchemists searching for an elixir of immortality.

etymologyHint: To fan 扇 the flames 火; 扇 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 火 (fire) reflects the literal act of fanning flames to make them burn hotter.
扇 means 'fan'; paired with fire, the image of fanning flames is extended metaphorically to 'stirring up' emotions or unrest in people.

example.hanzi: 他煽动大家闹事。
example.pinyin: Tā shāndòng dàjiā nàoshì.
example.english: He incited everyone to cause trouble.
example.fact: 煽情 (shānqíng, literally 'to fan up emotion') describes media or speeches that deliberately try to manipulate the audience's feelings — a common critical term in Chinese film and TV reviews.

example.hanzi: 用肥皂洗手可以去除细菌。
example.pinyin: Yòng féizào xǐshǒu kěyǐ qùchú xìjūn.
example.english: Washing hands with soap can remove germs.
example.fact: Handwashing with soap (肥皂, féizào) is one of the most effective, low-cost ways to prevent the spread of infectious disease, which is why global health campaigns like Global Handwashing Day, observed every October 15, promote it worldwide.

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 舵 (a rudder) is a part of a boat.
它 (tā) gives a sound only distantly related to duò today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 船长掌舵,带领船员前进。
example.pinyin: Chuánzhǎng zhǎngduò, dàilǐng chuányuán qiánjìn.
example.english: The captain steers the helm, leading the crew forward.
example.fact: 掌舵 (zhǎngduò, literally 'to hold the rudder') is commonly used metaphorically in Chinese to describe leading an organization or country through difficult times, much like the English idiom 'at the helm.'

meanings: used in 囉嗦|啰嗦[luo1 suo5]

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嗦 (as in 哆嗦/啰嗦) is built from the mouth, the source of speech and sound.
索 (suǒ) gives a sound close to suo, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他冻得直哆嗦。
example.pinyin: Tā dòng de zhí duōsuo.
example.english: He was shivering from the cold.
example.fact: 嗦 almost always appears in the neutral-tone second syllable of words like 哆嗦 (duōsuo, 'to shiver') and 啰嗦 (luōsuo, 'long-winded, nagging') — it essentially never carries independent meaning on its own in modern Mandarin.

meanings: a legendary animal with short forelegs which rode a wolf

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 狈 is a legendary wolf-like beast.
贝 (bèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 狈's reading.

example.hanzi: 他被雨淋得很狼狈。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi yǔ lín de hěn lángbèi.
example.english: He got caught in the rain and looked utterly disheveled.
example.fact: 狼狈 (lángbèi) references a legendary pair of animals, 狼 (wolf) and 狈, said to be helpless without each other — 狈 supposedly had short front legs and needed to ride on the wolf's back, making the pair a metaphor for an awkward predicament.

components.note: 革 (leather) — 靴 (boots) were traditionally made of leather.
化 (huà) gives a sound only distantly related to xuē today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 冬天他喜欢穿靴子。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān tā xǐhuān chuān xuēzi.
example.english: In winter he likes to wear boots.
example.fact: 靴 carries the leather radical 革, distinguishing traditional boots from ordinary shoes 鞋 — both share the same radical since footwear was historically made primarily from leather or hide.

meanings: to cover with the hand (one's eyes, nose or ears)
etymologyHint: To resist 吾 by hand 扌; 吾 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand radical) shows that 捂 describes an action done with the hand.
吾 is a classical word for 'I, me'; here it mainly fills out the character's sound and shape rather than contributing to the meaning of 'covering.'

example.hanzi: 她惊讶地捂住了嘴。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngyà de wǔ zhù le zuǐ.
example.english: She covered her mouth in surprise.
example.fact: 捂 is a relatively modern, colloquial character, commonly used in everyday spoken Mandarin for physically covering something with your hand or body, such as your mouth or ears, rather than in formal written Chinese.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 疮 (a sore, a boil) is a symptom tied to illness.
仓 (cāng) gives a sound only distantly related to chuāng today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他的手上长了冻疮。
example.pinyin: Tā de shǒu shàng zhǎng le dòngchuāng.
example.english: He developed frostbite sores on his hands.
example.fact: 疮 uses the sickness radical 疒, part of a large family of Chinese characters describing wounds and ailments — many of which, like 疮 and 疤 (scar), group together in dictionaries under the same radical section.

components.note: 阝 (place, town) — 郝 traces to an ancient place name, now a surname.
赤 (chì) gives a sound only distantly related to hǎo today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 郝先生是我们的新同事。
example.pinyin: Hǎo xiānsheng shì wǒmen de xīn tóngshì.
example.english: Mr. Hao is our new colleague.
example.fact: 郝 carries the 'place' radical 阝, common in surnames derived from ancient place names or fiefs, such as 郑, 邓, and 邹 — a strong hint that a surname originated as a territorial name in ancient China.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苛 (harsh, petty) was likely rooted in the image of a troublesome weed.
可 (kě) gives a sound close to kē, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 老板对员工的要求非常苛刻。
example.pinyin: Lǎobǎn duì yuángōng de yāoqiú fēicháng kēkè.
example.english: The boss's demands on employees are extremely harsh.
example.fact: The idiom 苛政猛于虎 ('harsh government is fiercer than a tiger') comes from a story in the Confucian classic 礼记 (Book of Rites), about a widow who feared cruel officials more than the tigers that had already killed her family.

components.note: 禾 (cereal, grain, rice; plant, stalk) — 秽 (filth) traces back to weeds choking a grain field.
岁 (suì) gives a sound distantly related to huì, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 街道上到处都是污秽的垃圾。
example.pinyin: Jiēdào shàng dàochù dōu shì wūhuì de lājī.
example.english: The streets are covered in filthy trash everywhere.
example.fact: 秽 carries the grain radical 禾, reflecting its ancient root sense of 'weeds growing among crops' — over time the meaning broadened from literal agricultural weeds to any kind of filth or moral corruption.

meanings: used in the transliteration of people's names

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 茜 (the madder plant) is a plant.
西 (xī) gives a sound only distantly related to qiàn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 茜草的根可以用来做红色染料。
example.pinyin: Qiàncǎo de gēn kěyǐ yòng lái zuò hóngsè rǎnliào.
example.english: The roots of the madder plant can be used to make red dye.
example.fact: The madder plant (茜草) has been used since ancient times across Asia and Europe as a source of natural red dye — the same plant family gave rise to the pigment name 'madder' and the dye alizarin, before synthetic dyes largely replaced it in the 19th century.

meanings: to rub or roll between the hands
to rub or roll between the hands or fingers

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 搓 (to rub, to roll between the hands) is an act done with the hand.
差 (chà) gives a sound only distantly related to cuō today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他搓着手取暖。
example.pinyin: Tā cuō zhe shǒu qǔnuǎn.
example.english: He rubbed his hands together to keep warm.
example.fact: 搓 is the specific verb Chinese uses for rubbing or rolling something repeatedly between the palms, such as warming your hands or rolling dough into balls (搓汤圆, hand-rolling rice-ball dumplings) — distinct from other rubbing verbs like 擦 (to wipe).

meanings: herb used to keep insects away

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 芸 (as in 芸芸众生) traces to the lush growth of vegetation.
云 (yún) gives the sound — an exact match with 芸's reading.

example.hanzi: 佛教常用'芸芸众生'来形容普通人。
example.pinyin: Fójiào chángyòng 'yúnyún zhòngshēng' lái xíngróng pǔtōng rén.
example.english: Buddhism often uses the phrase 'the mass of sentient beings' to describe ordinary people.
example.fact: 芸芸众生 (yúnyún zhòngshēng), a Buddhist-influenced idiom for the countless ordinary beings of the world, originally described the lush, teeming growth of plants (芸, 'luxuriant vegetation') before being extended to living creatures.

components.note: 酉 (wine) — 酱 (a fermented paste) is a wine-and-fermentation product.
丬 (qiáng) gives a sound distantly related to jiàng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 北京烤鸭常常配甜面酱吃。
example.pinyin: Běijīng kǎoyā chángcháng pèi tiánmiànjiàng chī.
example.english: Beijing roast duck is often eaten with sweet bean sauce.
example.fact: 酱 gives its name to a huge family of fermented Chinese pastes and sauces — from 豆瓣酱 (fermented broad bean paste) to 甜面酱 (sweet flour paste) — many relying on fermentation techniques that predate soy sauce production by centuries.

etymologyHint: Someone 任 working for money 贝

components.note: 贝 (shell/money radical) marks 赁 as related to payment — ancient Chinese currency was originally cowrie shells.
任 means 'to appoint, to entrust'; combined with the money radical, it suggests entrusting property to someone in exchange for payment — renting or hiring.

example.hanzi: 公司租赁了一间办公室。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī zūlìn le yī jiān bàngōngshì.
example.english: The company leased an office.
example.fact: 租赁 (zūlìn) is the standard formal and legal term in Chinese for 'leasing' or 'renting,' commonly seen in contracts, real estate, and car-rental businesses (租赁公司, 'leasing company').

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — 檐 (eaves) are a wooden part of a roof's structure.
詹 (zhān) gives a sound distantly related to yán, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 雨水顺着屋檐往下流。
example.pinyin: Yǔshuǐ shùn zhe wūyán wǎng xià liú.
example.english: Rainwater flows down along the eaves of the roof.
example.fact: Traditional Chinese architecture often features dramatically overhanging eaves (屋檐) not just for looks but for function — they extend rainwater runoff away from the wooden structure and walls, protecting them from moisture damage.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饷 (a soldier's pay) historically bundled wages with food rations.
向 (xiàng) gives a sound close to xiǎng, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 士兵们领到了军饷。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen lǐngdào le jūnxiǎng.
example.english: The soldiers received their military pay.
example.fact: 饷 carries the food radical 饣, since a soldier's 军饷 (jūnxiǎng) historically included both wages and provisions — pay and food rations were often bundled together as one concept in pre-modern armies.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 蕉 (the banana plant) is a plant.
焦 (jiāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 蕉's reading.

example.hanzi: 猴子喜欢吃香蕉。
example.pinyin: Hóuzi xǐhuān chī xiāngjiāo.
example.english: Monkeys like to eat bananas.
example.fact: 蕉 carries the grass/plant radical 艹, even though banana 'trees' aren't really trees — botanically, the banana plant is the world's largest herbaceous flowering plant, with no true woody trunk.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铀 (uranium) is a metal.
由 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 铀's reading.

example.hanzi: 铀是制造核燃料的重要原料。
example.pinyin: Yóu shì zhìzào hé ránliào de zhòngyào yuánliào.
example.english: Uranium is an important raw material for making nuclear fuel.
example.fact: Uranium (铀, yóu) has an isotope, U-235, that can sustain a nuclear chain reaction, making it the key fuel for both nuclear power plants and, historically, the first atomic bombs.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苔 (moss) is a small plant.
台 (tái) gives the sound — an exact match with 苔's reading.

example.hanzi: 石头上长满了青苔。
example.pinyin: Shítou shàng zhǎng mǎn le qīngtái.
example.english: The rocks are covered in moss.
example.fact: In Traditional Chinese Medicine, doctors examine 舌苔 (shétāi, the coating on a patient's tongue) as a diagnostic sign — its color and thickness are believed to reflect digestion and internal health, a practice still used in TCM consultations today.

components.note: 攵 (to strike, to act) — 赦 (to pardon) is framed as an authoritative act.
赤 (chì) gives a sound only distantly related to shè today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 政府对部分囚犯实行了赦免。
example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ duì bùfèn qiúfàn shíxíng le shèmiǎn.
example.english: The government granted a pardon to some prisoners.
example.fact: 大赦 ('general amnesty') was a common practice by emperors in imperial China, often declared to mark auspicious occasions like a new reign or recovery from illness, releasing or pardoning large numbers of prisoners at once.

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 缎 (satin) is a woven silk fabric.
段 (duàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 缎's reading.

example.hanzi: 她穿了一条丝绸缎面裙子。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān le yī tiáo sīchóu duànmiàn qúnzi.
example.english: She wore a silk satin skirt.
example.fact: 缎 carries the silk radical 纟, part of a large family of Chinese characters describing textiles — silk production and trade were so central to the ancient Chinese economy that the Silk Road takes its name from this export.

meanings: side of a ship or an aircraft

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 舷 (the side of a boat) is a part of a boat.
玄 (xuán) gives a sound distantly related to xián, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 他站在船舷边看海。
example.pinyin: Tā zhàn zài chuánxián biān kàn hǎi.
example.english: He stood by the side of the ship, looking at the sea.
example.fact: 舷 carries the boat radical 舟, and its compound 左舷/右舷 (zuǒxián/yòuxián) correspond exactly to 'port' and 'starboard' in English nautical terminology — every seafaring language develops precise vocabulary for orientation at sea.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 筷 (chopsticks) are traditionally made of bamboo.
快 (kuài) gives the sound — an exact match with 筷's reading.

example.hanzi: 中国人吃饭习惯用筷子。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó rén chīfàn xíguàn yòng kuàizi.
example.english: Chinese people are accustomed to eating with chopsticks.
example.fact: Chopsticks (筷子, kuàizi) have been used in China for at least 3,000 years, and the character 筷 carries the bamboo radical 竹, since bamboo has traditionally been one of the most common materials for making them.

components.note: 月 (moon; month) — 朔 (the new moon) is a phase of the moon.
屰 (nì) is the true second component per 朔's decomposition (⿰屰月); its reading bears little resemblance to shuò, and the original sound link, if any, is unclear today.

example.hanzi: 农历每月初一叫朔日。
example.pinyin: Nónglì měi yuè chūyī jiào shuòrì.
example.english: The first day of each lunar month is called 'shuo day.'
example.fact: In the traditional Chinese lunar calendar, 朔 (shuò) designates the astronomical new moon, when the moon sits between the earth and sun and appears invisible — marking the start of each lunar month, still used to calculate holidays like Chinese New Year.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婪 (greed, avarice) is traditionally personified as a trait.
林 (lín) gives a sound distantly related to lán, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 他对金钱十分贪婪。
example.pinyin: Tā duì jīnqián shífēn tānlán.
example.english: He is extremely greedy for money.
example.fact: 婪 almost exclusively appears paired with 贪 in 贪婪 (tānlán, 'greedy'), rarely standing alone — a common pattern in Chinese where two synonyms combine into a single, stronger two-character word.

components.note: 糸 (thread, silk) — 紊 (disorder) was originally about tangled threads.
文 (wén) gives a sound close to wěn, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 长期压力会导致内分泌紊乱。
example.pinyin: Chángqī yālì huì dǎozhì nèifēnmì wěnluàn.
example.english: Long-term stress can lead to hormonal imbalance.
example.fact: 紊乱 (wěnluàn) is common in medical Chinese, especially in the phrase 内分泌紊乱 ('hormonal/endocrine imbalance'), a frequent diagnosis discussed in health contexts relating to stress, diet, and sleep.

components.note: 厂 (cliff, building) — 厮 (a servant; to fight) is rooted in a building or workshop where menial work was done.
斯 (sī) gives the sound — an exact match with 厮's reading.

example.hanzi: 两军在战场上厮杀。
example.pinyin: Liǎng jūn zài zhànchǎng shàng sīshā.
example.english: The two armies fought fiercely on the battlefield.
example.fact: 厮杀 (sīshā) is common in Chinese historical novels and films for intense hand-to-hand combat between armies, while 厮 alone in older vernacular fiction like Water Margin (水浒传) could simply mean a young male servant.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婿 (a son-in-law) is a family role defined through marriage to a woman.
胥 (xū) gives a sound close to xù, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他是我最疼爱的女婿。
example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zuì téng'ài de nǚxu.
example.english: He is my most beloved son-in-law.
example.fact: 女婿 ('son-in-law') is a key term in Chinese family structure, and the relationship between a man and his wife's parents (岳父母) traditionally carries its own etiquette, distinct from blood relations.

components.note: 宀 (roof, house) — 寥 (scarce, empty) is framed as an empty house.
翏 (liù) gives a sound distantly related to liáo, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 会议室里只有寥寥几个人。
example.pinyin: Huìyìshì lǐ zhǐyǒu liáoliáo jǐ gè rén.
example.english: There were only a scant few people in the meeting room.
example.fact: 寥寥无几 (liáoliáo wújǐ, 'extremely few, scarcely any') reduplicates 寥 for emphasis, a very common Chinese pattern where doubling a character intensifies its meaning of scarcity.

components.note: 兢 doubles 克 ('to overcome, to restrain oneself'); the doubling suggests constant self-restraint and vigilance, fitting 兢's meaning of being extremely careful and conscientious.

example.hanzi: 他工作兢兢业业,从不懈怠。
example.pinyin: Tā gōngzuò jīngjīngyèyè, cóng bù xièdài.
example.english: He works conscientiously and diligently, never slacking off.
example.fact: 兢兢业业 (jīngjīngyèyè) is a common four-character idiom praising diligent, careful work — frequently used in Chinese performance reviews and official commendations to describe a model employee.

components.note: 米 (rice) — 糙 (coarse, unrefined) describes unpolished rice/grain.
造 (zào) gives a sound distantly related to cāo, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 这块木板表面很粗糙。
example.pinyin: Zhè kuài mùbǎn biǎomiàn hěn cūcāo.
example.english: The surface of this wooden board is very rough.
example.fact: 糙米 ('brown rice') keeps its bran and germ layer, unlike polished white rice, which is why it retains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals — the character 糙 carries the rice radical 米, tying 'roughness' directly to unrefined grain.

components.note: 卜 (divination) — 卦 (a divinatory diagram) belongs to fortune-telling.
圭 (guī) gives a sound distantly related to guà, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 太极图和八卦是中国传统文化的象征。
example.pinyin: Tàijítú hé bāguà shì Zhōngguó chuántǒng wénhuà de xiàngzhēng.
example.english: The taiji diagram and the Eight Trigrams are symbols of traditional Chinese culture.
example.fact: 八卦 (bāguà, 'the Eight Trigrams') are a foundational symbol system in the ancient Chinese classic 易经 (the Book of Changes), each trigram built from three stacked broken or unbroken lines representing combinations of yin and yang.

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — 槐 (the scholar tree) is a tree.
鬼 (guǐ) gives a sound only distantly related to huái today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 老槐树已经有上百年的历史了。
example.pinyin: Lǎo huáishù yǐjīng yǒu shàng bǎi nián de lìshǐ le.
example.english: The old locust tree has a history of over a hundred years.
example.fact: The Chinese scholar tree (槐树, huáishù) was historically planted in large numbers along Beijing's hutong lanes and is closely associated with the city's old imperial-era streetscape, with many centuries-old specimens still protected today.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扒 (to scratch, to dig at) is an act done with the hand/paw.
八 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 扒's reading.

example.hanzi: 小狗用爪子扒土。
example.pinyin: Xiǎogǒu yòng zhuǎzi bā tǔ.
example.english: The puppy scratches at the dirt with its paws.
example.fact: 扒 has two common readings with different senses: bā, as in scratching or peeling, and pá, as in 扒手 (páshǒu, 'pickpocket') — another example of how a tone change can signal a shift in meaning for the same character.

components.note: 衣 (clothing) — 裴 describes the flowing look of a long robe.
非 (fēi) gives a sound distantly related to péi, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 裴先生是一位历史学教授。
example.pinyin: Péi xiānsheng shì yī wèi lìshǐxué jiàoshòu.
example.english: Mr. Pei is a history professor.
example.fact: 裴 carries the clothing radical 衣, and its rare literary sense describes the flowing, elegant look of a long robe — fitting for a character whose main modern use is as a relatively uncommon Chinese surname.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, ritual) — 祀 (to sacrifice, to worship) is a ritual act.
巳 (sì) gives the sound — an exact match with 祀's reading.

example.hanzi: 古人常常举行祭祀活动。
example.pinyin: Gǔrén chángcháng jǔxíng jìsì huódòng.
example.english: Ancient people often held sacrificial ceremonies.
example.fact: 祀 carries the spirit/ritual radical 礻, found in many characters related to worship and the supernatural, such as 神 (god, spirit) and 祝 (to bless) — 祭祀 (ritual sacrifice) was one of the most important state activities in ancient Chinese dynasties.

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 埔 (a plain, a wharf) names a stretch of land.
甫 (fǔ) gives a sound distantly related to bù, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 黄埔军校培养了许多军事人才。
example.pinyin: Huángpǔ jūnxiào péiyǎng le xǔduō jūnshì réncái.
example.english: Whampoa Military Academy trained many military talents.
example.fact: 黄埔军校 (the Whampoa Military Academy), founded in Guangzhou in 1924 with Soviet assistance, trained many key military leaders on both the Nationalist and Communist sides of 20th-century Chinese history, including Chiang Kai-shek as its first commandant.

components.note: 糸 (thread, silk) — 絮 (cotton wadding) is a soft fiber related to thread.
如 (rú) gives a sound distantly related to xù, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 奶奶总是絮叨个不停。
example.pinyin: Nǎinai zǒng shì xùdao gè bù tíng.
example.english: Grandma always rambles on endlessly.
example.fact: 絮叨 (xùdao, 'to nag, to ramble') metaphorically compares long-winded talk to loose, drifting cotton wadding (絮) — soft, fluffy, and seemingly endless, much like the willow catkins Chinese poetry calls 柳絮.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 芭 (as in 芭蕉, banana) is a plant.
巴 (bā) gives the sound — an exact match with 芭's reading.

example.hanzi: 她从小学习芭蕾舞。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngxiǎo xuéxí bālěiwǔ.
example.english: She has studied ballet since childhood.
example.fact: 芭蕾 (bāléi, 'ballet') is a phonetic transliteration into Chinese, chosen for how the characters sound rather than their literal meanings — a common strategy for borrowing foreign loanwords with no natural Chinese equivalent.

example.hanzi: 他把文件放进抽屉里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ wénjiàn fàng jìn chōuti lǐ.
example.english: He put the documents into the drawer.
example.fact: 屉 also names the removable, perforated trays stacked inside a Chinese bamboo steamer (蒸屉, zhēngtì) — the same character bridges two seemingly different objects, a desk drawer and a steamer tray, united by the idea of a shallow, removable compartment.

meanings: used in 癱瘓|瘫痪[tan1 huan4]

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痪 (as in 瘫痪, paralysis) is a medical condition.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 痪's reading.

example.hanzi: 那场事故让他下肢瘫痪。
example.pinyin: Nà chǎng shìgù ràng tā xiàzhī tānhuàn.
example.english: That accident left his legs paralyzed.
example.fact: 痪 never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists solely inside 瘫痪 (tānhuàn, 'paralysis'), a word that can also be used metaphorically, such as 交通瘫痪 ('traffic gridlock').

etymologyHint: To look like 肖 rain 雨; 肖 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 雨 (rain) places the character in the domain of sky and weather.
肖 mainly fills out the character's sound and shape here rather than adding to its meaning of 'sky, clouds.'

example.hanzi: 火箭直冲云霄。
example.pinyin: Huǒjiàn zhí chōng yúnxiāo.
example.english: The rocket shot straight up into the sky.
example.fact: The idiom 九霄云外 ('beyond the ninth heaven') describes something impossibly far away or completely forgotten, drawing on the traditional Chinese cosmological idea that the sky was divided into nine layers.

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 绽 (to split open at a seam) describes thread giving way.
定 (dìng) gives a sound only distantly related to zhàn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 花朵在春天绽放。
example.pinyin: Huāduǒ zài chūntiān zhànfàng.
example.english: Flowers bloom in spring.
example.fact: 破绽 (pòzhàn), literally 'a torn seam,' is commonly used metaphorically in Chinese to mean a flaw or giveaway in a story, plan, or lie — much like the English idea of something 'coming apart at the seams.'

components.note: 宀 (roof, house) — 宵 (night) is framed as the dark hours spent inside one's home.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound close to xiāo, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 元宵节人们会吃汤圆、赏花灯。
example.pinyin: Yuánxiāo Jié rénmen huì chī tāngyuán, shǎng huādēng.
example.english: During the Lantern Festival, people eat rice-ball dumplings and admire lanterns.
example.fact: 元宵节 (the Lantern Festival) falls on the 15th day of the first lunar month and marks the traditional end of Chinese New Year celebrations, featuring lantern displays and round glutinous rice balls symbolizing family unity.

etymologyHint: A place 口 where people hope 巴 to settle

components.note: The upper enclosure represents city walls surrounding a settlement.
The lower part is thought to derive from the image of a kneeling person, representing the inhabitants living within the walled town.

example.hanzi: 城邑是古代重要的行政单位。
example.pinyin: Chéngyì shì gǔdài zhòngyào de xíngzhèng dānwèi.
example.english: Walled towns were important administrative units in ancient times.
example.fact: 邑 is the original, full form of the 'place' radical 阝 seen on the right side of characters like 郑, 邹, and 郝 — when 邑 stands alone it means a walled town or city.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — 霖 (a long, heavy rain) is a kind of rain.
林 (lín) gives the sound — an exact match with 霖's reading.

example.hanzi: 久旱的土地终于迎来了甘霖。
example.pinyin: Jiǔhàn de tǔdì zhōngyú yíngláile gānlín.
example.english: The long-parched land finally welcomed timely, life-giving rain.
example.fact: 甘霖 (gānlín, literally 'sweet, welcome rain') is often used metaphorically in Chinese to describe any timely help or relief that arrives just when badly needed, extending the literal image of rain ending a drought.

meanings: branch in road, river, mountain range etc
etymologyHint: A road being split 分 by a mountain 山

components.note: 分 means 'to divide, to split.'
山 (mountain) suggests the terrain being divided — as when a mountain path splits into a fork.

example.hanzi: 走到岔路口,他不知道该往哪边走。
example.pinyin: Zǒu dào chàlùkǒu, tā bù zhīdào gāi wǎng nǎbiān zǒu.
example.english: Arriving at the fork in the road, he didn't know which way to go.
example.fact: 打岔 (dǎchà, literally 'to hit a fork') is a common colloquial term for interrupting someone mid-conversation, extending the image of a road splitting off in a different direction to a conversation being derailed.

components.note: 饣 (food) — 饵 (bait; a snack) is something edible or related to food.
耳 (ěr) gives the sound — an exact match with 饵's reading.

example.hanzi: 他在鱼钩上挂了鱼饵。
example.pinyin: Tā zài yúgōu shàng guà le yúěr.
example.english: He put bait on the fishhook.
example.fact: 饵 carries the food radical 饣, and its extended meaning of 'to entice, to lure' (诱饵, 'bait') treats tempting someone into a trap the same way a fisherman uses food to lure a fish — a metaphor shared across many languages.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 茄 (the eggplant) is a plant.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 茄's reading.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢抽雪茄。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuān chōu xuějiā.
example.english: He likes to smoke cigars.
example.fact: 茄 has two very different everyday uses depending on pronunciation: qié in 茄子 ('eggplant'), and jiā in 雪茄 (xuějiā, literally 'snow eggplant,' a phonetic transliteration for 'cigar') — the cigar sense has nothing to do with eggplants and was chosen purely for its sound.

components.note: 韦 (tanned leather; surname) — 韧 (tough, pliable) describes tanned leather's resilience.
刃 (rèn) gives the sound — an exact match with 韧's reading.

example.hanzi: 竹子既坚硬又有韧性。
example.pinyin: Zhúzi jì jiānyìng yòu yǒu rènxìng.
example.english: Bamboo is both hard and resilient.
example.fact: 韧性 (rènxìng, 'resilience, toughness') is a materials-science term for a material's ability to bend or absorb stress without breaking — bamboo is frequently cited in Chinese culture as a natural symbol of this quality.

components.note: 王 (jade) — 琪 (a fine jade) is a type of jade.
其 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 琪's reading.

example.hanzi: 她的名字里有一个'琪'字,寓意美好。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi lǐ yǒu yī gè 'qí' zì, yùyì měihǎo.
example.english: Her name contains the character 'qi,' carrying an auspicious meaning.
example.fact: 琪 carries the jade radical 王 (a compact form of 玉), part of a family of characters used almost exclusively in given names for their precious, auspicious connotations, such as 珍, 瑶, and 玲.

components.note: 阝 (place, town) — 邹 was the name of an ancient state, now a surname derived from a place.
刍 (chú) gives a sound only distantly related to zōu today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 邹是一个常见的中国姓氏。
example.pinyin: Zōu shì yī gè chángjiàn de Zhōngguó xìngshì.
example.english: Zou is a common Chinese surname.
example.fact: 邹 was the name of a small ancient state during the Zhou dynasty period, located in what is now Shandong province — near the birthplace of Mencius, the second most important Confucian philosopher after Confucius himself.

components.note: 王 (jade) — 瑚 (as in 珊瑚, coral) was classed with precious, jade-like materials.
胡 (hú) gives the sound — an exact match with 瑚's reading.

example.hanzi: 珊瑚礁是海洋生物的家园。
example.pinyin: Shānhújiāo shì hǎiyáng shēngwù de jiāyuán.
example.english: Coral reefs are home to marine life.
example.fact: 瑚 never appears alone in modern Chinese — it exists solely as the second syllable of 珊瑚 ('coral'). Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor yet support roughly a quarter of all known marine species, making them among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth.

components.note: 心 (heart, mind) — 憋 (to suppress a feeling) is an internal, emotional state.
敝 (bì) gives a sound distantly related to biē, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 他心里有话,却憋着不说。
example.pinyin: Tā xīnlǐ yǒu huà, què biē zhe bù shuō.
example.english: He had something to say, but held it in and didn't speak.
example.fact: 憋气 (biēqì) has two related senses: literally 'to hold your breath' (as underwater), and figuratively 'to feel stifled or frustrated' when forced to suppress an emotion — 憋 carries the heart radical 心 to mark it as an internal, emotional state.

components.note: 歹 (corpse; death; evil, depraved, wicked) — 殆 (dangerous, near death) is tied to death and peril.
台 (tái) gives a sound distantly related to dài, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 病情十分危殆。
example.pinyin: Bìngqíng shífēn wēidài.
example.english: The medical condition is extremely critical.
