example.fact: 殆 appears in the famous line from Sun Tzu's Art of War, 知彼知己，百战不殆 ('know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril') — one of the most quoted strategic maxims in Chinese and world military thought.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 噜 (as in 咕噜, a gurgling sound) is built from the mouth, the source of the sound.
鲁 (lǔ) gives a sound close to lū, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他肚子饿得咕噜咕噜叫。
example.pinyin: Tā dùzi è de gūlū gūlū jiào.
example.english: His stomach growled from hunger.
example.fact: 噜 is primarily an onomatopoeic character, used to represent sounds like a growling stomach (咕噜) — many Chinese characters built on the mouth radical 口 exist specifically to write out sounds rather than carry independent meaning.

components.note: 心 (heart, mind) — 忒 (too, excessively) is used to intensify a feeling or state.
弋 (yì) gives a sound only distantly related to tè today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 这件事忒麻烦了。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì tè máfan le.
example.english: This matter is too much trouble.
example.fact: 忒 (tè) is a colloquial intensifier meaning 'too, excessively,' especially common in Beijing dialect as an alternative to the standard 太 (tài) — a good example of regional Mandarin variation in everyday speech.

components.note: 心 (heart, mind) — 忿 (anger, indignation) is an emotional state.
分 (fēn) gives a sound close to fèn, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他心中忿忿不平。
example.pinyin: Tā xīnzhōng fènfèn bùpíng.
example.english: He was filled with indignant resentment.
example.fact: 忿 and the more common 愤 (both fèn) are near-synonyms for anger — both are built on the heart radical (心/忄), reflecting how Chinese characters often locate emotional states in the heart rather than the head.

meanings: consecrate sacrificial vessels by smearing blood

components.note: 血 (blood) — 衅 traces to an ancient blood-sacrifice ritual.
半 (bàn) gives a sound only distantly related to xìn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他故意挑衅对方。
example.pinyin: Tā gùyì tiǎoxìn duìfāng.
example.english: He deliberately provoked the other side.
example.fact: 衅 originally referred to an ancient ritual of smearing fresh blood on a sacrificial vessel to consecrate it — its blood radical 血 preserves this ancient origin, even though its modern use in 挑衅 ('to provoke') is purely about starting conflict.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淳 (honest, unspoiled) is likened to pure, untainted water.
享 (xiǎng) gives a sound only distantly related to chún today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 山里的村民十分淳朴。
example.pinyin: Shān lǐ de cūnmín shífēn chúnpǔ.
example.english: The villagers in the mountains are very simple and honest.
example.fact: 淳朴 (chúnpǔ, 'simple and unaffected') is a common compliment in Chinese for people, especially from rural or traditional backgrounds, whose character is seen as genuine and uncorrupted by modern sophistication.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 悖 (contradictory, perverse) is a fault of reasoning, seated in the heart/mind.
孛 (bèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 悖's reading.

example.hanzi: 这个说法自相矛盾,是个悖论。
example.pinyin: Zhège shuōfǎ zì xiāng máodùn, shì gè bèilùn.
example.english: This statement contradicts itself; it's a paradox.
example.fact: 悖论 (bèilùn) is the standard Chinese term for 'paradox' in logic and philosophy, used for classic problems like 罗素悖论 (Russell's Paradox) in set theory.

components.note: 髟 (long hair) — 髦 (fashionable; a child's flowing hair) is rooted in hairstyle.
毛 (máo) gives the sound — an exact match with 髦's reading.

example.hanzi: 她穿得很时髦。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān de hěn shímáo.
example.english: She dresses very fashionably.
example.fact: 髦 carries the hair radical 髟, seen atop characters like 发 (hair) and 鬃 (mane); its extension to mean 'fashionable' (时髦, shímáo) likely traces back to how a stylish hairstyle has long marked being trendy.

components.note: 攵 (to strike, to act) — 孜 (as in 孜孜, diligent) frames diligence as a sustained effort.
子 (zi) gives a sound close to zī, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他孜孜不倦地学习汉语。
example.pinyin: Tā zīzī bùjuàn de xuéxí Hànyǔ.
example.english: He studies Chinese diligently and tirelessly.
example.fact: 孜 essentially never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it's used almost exclusively in the reduplicated form 孜孜 or the idiom 孜孜不倦 ('diligent and untiring'), often used to praise dedicated students or workers.

meanings: short name for Guangdong 廣東|广东[Guang3 dong1]

example.hanzi: 粤语是广东最有代表性的方言。
example.pinyin: Yuèyǔ shì Guǎngdōng zuì yǒu dàibiǎoxìng de fāngyán.
example.english: Cantonese is the most representative dialect of Guangdong.
example.fact: 粤语 (Cantonese) preserves more of the consonant endings of Middle Chinese than Standard Mandarin does, and with six to nine tones depending on classification, it has one of the most complex tone systems among the major Chinese language varieties.

meanings: (bound form) a defile; a narrow pass

components.note: 阝 (place, town) — 隘 (narrow, confined) describes a constricted mountain pass.
益 (yì) gives a sound only distantly related to ài today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他的想法有些狭隘。
example.pinyin: Tā de xiǎngfǎ yǒuxiē xiáài.
example.english: His thinking is somewhat narrow-minded.
example.fact: 隘 carries the hill radical 阝, and its sense of a narrow mountain pass extends naturally to 'narrow-minded' (狭隘) — many strategic passes in Chinese history controlled entire regions precisely because they were narrow chokepoints.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 濒 (to border on, to verge on) is rooted in the image of a riverbank.
频 (pín) gives a sound distantly related to bīn, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 大熊猫曾经是濒危动物。
example.pinyin: Dà xióngmāo céngjīng shì bīnwēi dòngwù.
example.english: The giant panda used to be an endangered animal.
example.fact: The giant panda was reclassified by the IUCN from 'endangered' to the less severe 'vulnerable' in 2016, thanks to decades of conservation efforts in China.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铮 (a clanging sound) is the ring of struck metal.
争 (zhēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 铮's reading.

example.hanzi: 他是个铁骨铮铮的硬汉。
example.pinyin: Tā shì gè tiěgǔ zhēngzhēng de yìnghàn.
example.english: He is an unyielding tough guy of iron will.
example.fact: 铁骨铮铮 (tiěgǔ zhēngzhēng), literally 'iron bones that clang,' is a vivid idiom praising someone's unyielding moral integrity, comparing a person's resolve to the ringing sound of struck metal.

etymologyHint: Leftover 奇 farmland 田; 奇 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 田 (farmland) marks the character's original meaning of an irregular, leftover strip of field.
奇 means 'odd, strange'; combined with farmland, it evokes an oddly-shaped or leftover plot of land, extended to mean anything abnormal or irregular.

example.hanzi: 这棵植物长得有些畸形。
example.pinyin: Zhè kē zhíwù zhǎng de yǒuxiē jīxíng.
example.english: This plant has grown somewhat deformed.
example.fact: 畸变 (jībiàn, 'distortion') is a technical term used in photography and optics for lens distortion, where straight lines in an image appear curved — the same character used for biological abnormality (畸形) also describes this optical imperfection.

meanings: to scrape the meat from bones

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剔 (to pick out, to scrape away) is done with a blade.
易 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to tī, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他对食物很挑剔。
example.pinyin: Tā duì shíwù hěn tiāotī.
example.english: He is very picky about food.
example.fact: 挑剔 (tiāotī, 'to nitpick, to be fussy') combines two verbs both meaning 'to pick out' — one hand-related (挑) and one with the knife radical 刂 (剔, 'to scrape away') — together intensifying the sense of overly critical selectiveness.

meanings: (bound form) low area within a surrounding barrier

components.note: 土 (earth, soil) — 坞 (a dock, an embankment) is an earthen structure.
乌 (wū) gives a sound close to wù, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这艘船正在船坞里维修。
example.pinyin: Zhè sōu chuán zhèngzài chuánwù lǐ wéixiū.
example.english: This ship is being repaired in the shipyard.
example.fact: 船坞 (chuánwù, 'dry dock, shipyard') refers to the walled or enclosed structure where ships are built or repaired out of water, carrying 坞's core sense of an earthen embankment or enclosed space.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 篱 (a fence) is traditionally woven from bamboo.
离 (lí) gives the sound — an exact match with 篱's reading.

example.hanzi: 院子周围围着一圈篱笆。
example.pinyin: Yuànzi zhōuwéi wéi zhe yī quān líba.
example.english: The yard is surrounded by a fence.
example.fact: 篱笆 (líba, 'fence') carries the bamboo radical 竹, reflecting how traditional rural Chinese fences were most commonly woven from bamboo or thin wooden strips rather than built from stone or brick.

meanings: (bound form) shallow lake (usu. in place names)

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淀 (shallow, silty water) is a body of water.
定 (dìng) gives a sound distantly related to diàn, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 土豆里含有大量淀粉。
example.pinyin: Tǔdòu lǐ hányǒu dàliàng diànfěn.
example.english: Potatoes contain a large amount of starch.
example.fact: 淀粉 (diànfěn, 'starch') gets its name from the way starch particles settle and precipitate (沉淀, chéndiàn) out of a water suspension during traditional extraction —淀 originally described this kind of shallow, sediment-collecting water.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 蓦 (suddenly) is paired here with a horse's abrupt start.
莫 (mò) gives the sound — an exact match with 蓦's reading.

example.hanzi: 他蓦然回首,发现她就在灯火阑珊处。
example.pinyin: Tā mòrán huíshǒu, fāxiàn tā jiù zài dēnghuǒ lánshān chù.
example.english: He suddenly turned back and found her right there where the lights were dim.
example.fact: 蓦然回首 ('suddenly turning to look back') comes from a famous line in a Song dynasty poem by Xin Qiji, and remains one of the most quoted phrases in Chinese literature for an unexpected moment of realization.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唬 (to bluff, to intimidate) is done through the mouth, evoking a tiger's roar.
虎 (hǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 唬's reading.

example.hanzi: 他只是在唬人,别害怕。
example.pinyin: Tā zhǐshì zài hǔ rén, bié hàipà.
example.english: He's just trying to bluff you; don't be afraid.
example.fact: 唬 combines the mouth radical 口 with 虎 (tiger), literally evoking the terrifying roar of a tiger — extended in modern Mandarin to mean bluffing or intimidating someone without real substance behind the threat.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锣 (a gong) is a metal instrument.
罗 (luō) gives a sound close to luó, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 春节时人们敲锣打鼓庆祝。
example.pinyin: Chūnjié shí rénmen qiāoluó dǎgǔ qìngzhù.
example.english: During Chinese New Year, people beat gongs and drums to celebrate.
example.fact: 敲锣打鼓 ('beating gongs and drums') is a traditional way to create a festive, celebratory atmosphere in China, commonly heard during lion dances, parades, and Lunar New Year festivities.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 汀 (a sandbar, a riverbank) is a feature of water.
丁 (dīng) gives a sound distantly related to tīng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 江边的沙汀上有几只白鹭。
example.pinyin: Jiāngbiān de shātīng shàng yǒu jǐ zhī báilù.
example.english: There are a few egrets on the sandbar by the river.
example.fact: 汀 is a predominantly literary and poetic character for a small sandbar or flat riverbank, frequently appearing in classical Chinese landscape poetry rather than everyday spoken Mandarin.

components.note: 足 (foot) — 趾 (the toe) is a part of the foot.
止 (zhǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 趾's reading.

example.hanzi: 她不小心撞伤了脚趾。
example.pinyin: Tā bù xiǎoxīn zhuàngshāng le jiǎozhǐ.
example.english: She accidentally injured her toe.
example.fact: 趾 carries the foot radical 足, distinguishing it from 指 (zhǐ, 'finger,' with the hand radical 扌) — the two characters are exact homophones, differentiated only by which radical marks whether you mean a toe or a finger.

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 缉 (to sew in close stitches; to track down) traces to needlework with thread.
咠 (qì) gives a sound distantly related to jī, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 警方对逃犯发出了通缉令。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng duì táofàn fāchū le tōngjī lìng.
example.english: The police issued a wanted notice for the fugitive.
example.fact: 通缉令 (tōngjī lìng, 'wanted notice') is the standard Chinese legal term for a police bulletin seeking a fugitive's capture, extending 缉's original sewing-related meaning of 'tracking down loose threads' to 'tracking down a criminal.'

components.note: 女 (woman) — 嫦 (as in 嫦娥) names a legendary woman.
常 (cháng) gives the sound — an exact match with 嫦's reading.

example.hanzi: 嫦娥是中国神话中的月亮女神。
example.pinyin: Cháng'é shì Zhōngguó shénhuà zhōng de yuèliang nǚshén.
example.english: Chang'e is the moon goddess in Chinese mythology.
example.fact: China's lunar exploration program is named 嫦娥工程 after this mythological moon goddess, and its Chang'e-4 mission achieved the first-ever soft landing on the far side of the Moon in January 2019.

meanings: to pour wine or tea into a cup

components.note: 斗 (measuring cup) — 斟 (to pour wine or tea) is done with a measuring ladle/cup.
甚 (shén) gives a sound distantly related to zhēn, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他仔细斟酌每一个字。
example.pinyin: Tā zǐxì zhēnzhuó měi yī gè zì.
example.english: He carefully deliberated over every word.
example.fact: 斟酌 (zhēnzhuó), literally 'to pour and measure wine,' is used metaphorically in Chinese to mean carefully weighing one's words or decisions — comparing careful thought to the precise pouring of wine into a cup.

components.note: 革 (leather) — 鞍 (a saddle) is traditionally made of leather.
安 (ān) gives the sound — an exact match with 鞍's reading.

example.hanzi: 骑马前要先系好马鞍。
example.pinyin: Qímǎ qián yào xiān jì hǎo mǎ'ān.
example.english: Before riding a horse, you must first secure the saddle.
example.fact: 鞍山, a major industrial city in Liaoning province, is named for a nearby mountain whose twin peaks resemble the shape of a saddle (鞍) — one of many Chinese place names taken directly from the landscape's appearance.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 扳 (to pull, to lever) is an act done with the hand.
反 (fǎn) gives a sound distantly related to bān, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他用扳手拧紧了螺丝。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng bānshou nǐngjǐn le luósī.
example.english: He used a wrench to tighten the screw.
example.fact: 扳回 (bānhuí, 'to pull back, to turn around') is often used in sports commentary to describe a team clawing back a losing score, extending the literal image of pulling a lever, like a wrench (扳手), back into position.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拴 (to tie up, to fasten) is an act done with the hand.
全 (quán) gives a sound distantly related to shuān, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 他把狗拴在树上。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ gǒu shuān zài shù shàng.
example.english: He tied the dog to the tree.
example.fact: 拴 specifically describes tying something with a rope or leash to fasten it in place, and its idiomatic use in phrases like 拴住一个人的心 ('to tie down someone's heart') extends the image to emotional devotion.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诅 (to curse) is done through speech.
且 (qiě) gives a sound only distantly related to zǔ today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 她在心里诅咒那个骗子。
example.pinyin: Tā zài xīnlǐ zǔzhòu nàge piànzi.
example.english: In her heart, she cursed that swindler.
example.fact: 诅咒 (zǔzhòu, 'to curse') combines two characters both meaning 'curse, oath' and both carrying the speech radical 讠, reflecting that a curse in traditional belief was seen as a spoken act with real power to cause harm.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谟 (a plan, counsel) is conveyed through speech.
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to mó, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古代典籍中常用'谟'字表示谋略。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài diǎnjí zhōng chángyòng 'mó' zì biǎoshì móulüè.
example.english: In ancient classical texts, the character 'mo' is often used to mean a strategy or plan.
example.fact: 谟 is a rare, highly literary character for 'plan, counsel,' found in classical titles like the 大禹谟 ('Counsels of the Great Yu') chapter of the ancient Book of Documents (尚书), one of the Five Classics of Confucianism.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 呃 (a hiccup, a filler word) comes from the mouth.
厄 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 呃's reading.

example.hanzi: 他吃太快,打了一个呃。
example.pinyin: Tā chī tài kuài, dǎ le yī gè è.
example.english: He ate too fast and let out a burp.
example.fact: 呃 serves double duty in modern spoken Chinese — as a character for a hiccup or burp, and as a common filler interjection ('呃...') similar to English 'uh...', used when someone hesitates mid-sentence.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 懦 (cowardly, weak-willed) is a trait seated in the heart.
需 (xū) gives a sound only distantly related to nuò today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他做事总是很懦弱。
example.pinyin: Tā zuòshì zǒng shì hěn nuòruò.
example.english: He is always cowardly and weak-willed in how he handles things.
example.fact: 懦弱 (nuòruò, 'cowardly, weak-willed') carries the heart radical 忄 in 懦, marking timidity as an internal, emotional trait — the same radical family used for many words describing courage and fear in traditional Chinese thought.

meanings: to carry out or succeed in a scheme

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 逞 (to show off, to indulge) describes a kind of forward, unchecked behavior — walking ahead unchecked.
呈 (chéng) gives a sound close to chěng, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他总喜欢在别人面前逞强。
example.pinyin: Tā zǒng xǐhuān zài biérén miànqián chěngqiáng.
example.english: He always likes to show off his bravado in front of others.
example.fact: 得逞 (déchěng, 'to succeed in a scheme') almost always carries a negative connotation in Chinese, implying an underhanded or malicious plan has succeeded — unlike neutral success words like 成功.

etymologyHint: To use an ox 牛 to harvest 刂 grain 禾; 利 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 牛 (ox) reflects that oxen have traditionally pulled the plow.
利 means 'sharp, to cut'; combined with the ox, it evokes a sharp blade being dragged through soil by a draft animal — a plow.

example.hanzi: 农民用牛拉犁耕地。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín yòng niú lā lí gēngdì.
example.english: Farmers use oxen to pull the plow and till the fields.
example.fact: The ox-drawn plow with an iron plowshare was a major agricultural advance in ancient China, and its widespread adoption during the Warring States and Han periods significantly boosted farming productivity.

components.note: 忄 (heart, mind) — 忏 (to repent) is an inner, emotional act.
千 (qiān) gives a sound only distantly related to chàn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 他向朋友忏悔自己的错误。
example.pinyin: Tā xiàng péngyou chànhuǐ zìjǐ de cuòwù.
example.english: He confessed and repented his mistake to his friend.
example.fact: 忏悔 (chànhuǐ, 'to repent, to confess') is used in both religious contexts — Buddhist confession rituals and Christian confession alike — and secular contexts, showing how remorseful self-examination crosses multiple belief systems in Chinese usage.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拧 (to twist, to wring) is an act done with the hand.
宁 (níng) gives the sound — an exact match with 拧's reading.

example.hanzi: 她拧干了湿毛巾。
example.pinyin: Tā níng gān le shī máojīn.
example.english: She wrung the wet towel dry.
example.fact: 拧 is a rare character with three different tones and meanings depending on context: níng ('to twist, to wring'), nǐng ('to turn a knob the wrong way'), and nìng ('stubborn') — all sharing the same underlying idea of forceful rotation.

example.hanzi: 亥是十二地支的最后一个。
example.pinyin: Hài shì shí'èr dìzhī de zuìhòu yī gè.
example.english: Hai is the last of the twelve Earthly Branches.
example.fact: 亥 is the twelfth and final of the twelve Earthly Branches used in the Chinese zodiac, corresponding to the Pig — someone born in a 亥 year, such as 2019 or 2031, belongs to the Year of the Pig.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 佟 is a surname referring to a person/lineage.
冬 (dōng) gives a sound distantly related to tóng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 佟先生是这家公司的创始人。
example.pinyin: Tóng xiānsheng shì zhè jiā gōngsī de chuàngshǐrén.
example.english: Mr. Tong is the founder of this company.
example.fact: 佟 is a relatively uncommon Chinese surname today, but it was historically associated with prominent Manchu clans during the Qing dynasty, including families closely connected to the imperial court.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 叱 (to scold, to shout at) is done through the mouth.
匕 (bǐ) gives a sound distantly related to chì, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 老师严厉地叱责了迟到的学生。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī yánlì de chìzé le chídào de xuésheng.
example.english: The teacher sternly reprimanded the students who were late.
example.fact: The idiom 叱咤风云 (literally 'to shout and command the wind and clouds') describes someone with immense power and influence, often used for dominant historical or political figures.

components.note: 爫 (claw) — 舜 (a legendary sage-king) is remembered in an old graphic built partly from a claw-like mark.
舛 (chuǎn) gives a sound only distantly related to shùn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 尧、舜是中国传说中的贤明君主。
example.pinyin: Yáo, Shùn shì Zhōngguó chuánshuō zhōng de xiánmíng jūnzhǔ.
example.english: Yao and Shun are wise, legendary rulers in Chinese lore.
example.fact: 舜 is one of the legendary Five Emperors of ancient China and is celebrated in Confucian tradition as a model of virtue — according to legend, he was chosen as successor by Emperor Yao purely for his moral character, not heredity.

components.note: 纟 (thread, silk) — 绊 (to trip, a tether) traces to being caught by a cord or thread.
半 (bàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 绊's reading.

example.hanzi: 他被石头绊倒了。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi shítou bàndǎo le.
example.english: He was tripped by a rock.
example.fact: 羁绊 (jībàn, 'fetters, entanglements') is often used metaphorically in Chinese for emotional or circumstantial ties that hold someone back, extending 绊's literal meaning of a rope or obstacle that trips you up.

components.note: 龙 (dragon) — 龚 (respectful; to give) associates giving with the dragon, a symbol of authority.
共 (gòng) gives a sound close to gōng, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 龚先生对人一向恭敬有礼。
example.pinyin: Gōng xiānsheng duì rén yīxiàng gōngjìng yǒulǐ.
example.english: Mr. Gong is always respectful and polite to others.
example.fact: 龚 combines the dragon radical 龙 with 共 ('together'); though now mainly known as a surname, it historically carried connotations of reverence and giving, the dragon being a symbol of imperial authority.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 腮 (the cheek, the jaw) is a fleshy part of the face.
思 (sī) gives a sound distantly related to sāi, sharing the initial consonant but having drifted apart in vowel over time.

example.hanzi: 她涂了一点腮红,看起来很有气色。
example.pinyin: Tā tú le yīdiǎn sāihóng, kànqǐlái hěn yǒu qìsè.
example.english: She applied a bit of blush, and looks radiant.
example.fact: 腮红 (sāihóng, 'blush') is the standard Chinese cosmetics term for cheek makeup — 腮 names the cheek/jaw area on a person, while the same character (鱼腮, 'fish gills') also names a fish's gills, since both sit on the sides of the head.

meanings: (bound form) residence of a high-ranking official

components.note: 阝 (place, town) — 邸 (an official residence) is tied to a place.
氐 (dī) gives a sound close to dǐ, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 总统住在官邸里。
example.pinyin: Zǒngtǒng zhù zài guāndǐ lǐ.
example.english: The president lives in the official residence.
example.fact: 官邸 (guāndǐ, 'official residence') pairs historically with 邸报 (dǐbào), the court gazettes issued from officials' residences in imperial China — considered one of the world's earliest forms of a regularly published news bulletin, dating back over a thousand years.

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — 椒 (pepper, spice) is a plant/tree product.
叔 (shū) gives a sound only distantly related to jiāo today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 四川菜里常常放花椒。
example.pinyin: Sìchuān cài lǐ chángcháng fàng huājiāo.
example.english: Sichuan cuisine often includes Sichuan pepper.
example.fact: 花椒 (huājiāo, 'Sichuan pepper') isn't related to black pepper at all — it's the dried husk of a different plant, prized for producing the unique tingling, numbing sensation on the tongue (麻) that defines authentic Sichuan cuisine.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 蔚 (luxuriant, thick) describes lush plant growth.
尉 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 蔚's reading.

example.hanzi: 天空是一片蔚蓝。
example.pinyin: Tiānkōng shì yī piàn wèilán.
example.english: The sky is a stretch of azure blue.
example.fact: 蔚蓝 (wèilán, 'azure, deep sky blue') is a common poetic and descriptive term in Chinese for a clear, vivid blue sky or sea — 蔚 alone conveys a sense of rich, flourishing abundance that intensifies the color word 蓝.

etymologyHint: A deep 甚 lake 氵; 甚 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) grounds 湛's original meaning of deep, clear water.
甚 means 'very, extremely'; its reading (shèn) is only loosely close to zhàn's, so it likely contributes more to intensifying the meaning ('very deep') than to the sound.

example.hanzi: 这位医生的医术十分精湛。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi yīshēng de yīshù shífēn jīngzhàn.
example.english: This doctor's medical skill is extremely masterful.
example.fact: 精湛 (jīngzhàn, 'consummate, highly refined') is a common compliment in Chinese for exceptional skill or craftsmanship, extending 湛's original sense of deep, clear water to describe the depth of someone's expertise.

meanings: to go hunting (as winter sport in former times)

components.note: 犭 (dog, beast) — 狩 (to hunt) was traditionally associated with hunting dogs.
守 (shǒu) gives a sound close to shòu, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 古代帝王常常外出狩猎。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài dìwáng chángcháng wàichū shòuliè.
example.english: Ancient emperors often went out hunting.
example.fact: 狩猎 ('to hunt') in ancient China was often more than sport — imperial hunting expeditions doubled as displays of military readiness and royal authority, sometimes involving large retinues of soldiers and officials.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 眶 (the eye socket) is a part of the eye.
匡 (kuāng) gives a sound close to kuàng, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,她热泪盈眶。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā rèlèi yíngkuàng.
example.english: Hearing this news, her eyes brimmed with hot tears.
example.fact: 热泪盈眶 ('hot tears brimming in the eye sockets') is a common four-character idiom in Chinese for being moved to tears, frequently used in news reports and literature to describe emotional reactions to touching moments.

meanings: a wooden or bamboo pen for sheep or cattle

components.note: 木 (wood, tree) — 栈 (a warehouse, an inn) was traditionally built of wood, and 栈道 ('plank road') were literally wooden planks.
戋 (jiān) gives a sound only distantly related to zhàn today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 旅客们住进了一家客栈。
example.pinyin: Lǚkèmen zhù jìn le yī jiā kèzhàn.
example.english: The travelers checked into an inn.
example.fact: 栈道 ('plank roads') were wooden walkways built by suspending planks on brackets driven into cliff faces, an engineering technique ancient China used to cross the otherwise impassable mountains of Sichuan.

meanings: Osmunda regalis, a species of fern

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 薇 names a fern species, a plant.
微 (wēi) gives the sound — an exact match with 薇's reading.

example.hanzi: 花园里种满了蔷薇。
example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ zhòng mǎn le qiángwēi.
example.english: The garden is full of planted roses.
example.fact: 薇 rarely stands alone in modern Chinese — its most common appearance is in 蔷薇 (qiángwēi), the Chinese word for 'rose,' even though the character's original literal meaning refers to an unrelated fern species.

meanings: used in 骯髒|肮脏[ang1 zang1]

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 肮 (as in 肮脏, dirty) describes something unclean, grouped under the body/flesh radical here.
亢 (kàng) gives a sound distantly related to āng, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 这条河的水又黑又肮脏。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo hé de shuǐ yòu hēi yòu āngzāng.
example.english: This river's water is both black and filthy.
example.fact: 肮 never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it exists solely as the first syllable of 肮脏 (āngzāng, 'dirty'), a compound where, unusually, neither character carries an independent meaning outside the pair.

etymologyHint: Violent 暴 water 氵; 暴 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water) marks 瀑 as related to a body of moving water.
暴 (here read pù, identical to 瀑's own reading, as in 曝光 pùguāng) also conveys violent force, fitting the crash of falling water.

example.hanzi: 瀑布从高处飞流直下。
example.pinyin: Pùbù cóng gāochù fēiliú zhí xià.
example.english: The waterfall cascades straight down from a great height.
example.fact: Huangguoshu Waterfall in Guizhou province, one of China's largest and most famous waterfalls, has a drop of roughly 78 meters.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渣 (dregs, residue) is what's left over from a liquid.
查 (chá) gives a sound distantly related to zhā, sharing the same final but having drifted apart in initial consonant over time.

example.hanzi: 磨完豆浆剩下很多豆渣。
example.pinyin: Mó wán dòujiāng shèngxià hěn duō dòuzhā.
example.english: After grinding soy milk, a lot of bean dregs are left over.
example.fact: 渣 extends from its literal sense of 'dregs, residue' to a common modern slang insult, 渣男 (zhānán, 'scumbag man'), which became especially widespread in Chinese internet slang for a dishonest or unfaithful romantic partner.

components.note: 衤 (clothing) — 褂 (a jacket) is an item of clothing.
卦 (guà) gives the sound — an exact match with 褂's reading.

example.hanzi: 他穿着一件蓝色的大褂。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān zhe yī jiàn lánsè de dàguà.
example.english: He wore a blue long gown.
example.fact: 马褂 ('riding jacket') was a short, buttoned jacket traditionally worn over a long robe by Qing dynasty men, originally designed for horseback riding, and it remains recognizable in period films and traditional Tangzhuang-style clothing today.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 叽 (as in 叽叽喳喳, chirping) is built from the mouth, the source of the sound.
几 (jǐ) gives a sound close to jī, sharing the same sound and differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小鸟在树上叽叽喳喳地叫。
example.pinyin: Xiǎoniǎo zài shù shàng jījizhāzhā de jiào.
example.english: The little birds chirp and chatter in the tree.
example.fact: 叽叽喳喳 (jījizhāzhā) is an onomatopoeic Chinese phrase imitating the chirping of birds or the chatter of people talking rapidly and noisily all at once — a lively expression built entirely from the mouth radical 口.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 臀 (the buttocks) is a fleshy part of the body.
殿 (diàn) gives a sound only distantly related to tún today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 久坐对臀部和腰部都不好。
example.pinyin: Jiǔ zuò duì túnbù hé yāobù dōu bù hǎo.
example.english: Sitting for long periods is bad for both the buttocks and the lower back.
example.fact: 臀 carries the flesh radical ⺼, part of a large family of Chinese characters for body parts — its upper structure, 殿 ('palace hall'), is borrowed purely for sound and shape here, not meaning.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妞 (a girl) refers to a female person.
丑 (chǒu) gives a sound only distantly related to niū today, a connection that has faded over roughly three millennia of sound change.

example.hanzi: 那个小妞儿很聪明。
example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎo niūr hěn cōngmíng.
example.english: That little girl is very clever.
example.fact: 妞 is a colloquial, affectionate term for a young girl, especially common in northern Chinese dialects like Beijing Mandarin (妞儿, niūr, with its characteristic retroflex 'er' ending) — it carries a folksy, informal tone rarely used in formal writing.
